articles.title: Crochet novices in Friston create cascading poppy memorial
articles.summary: The friends took up crocheting a year ago before getting the whole village involved.
articles.body:
Novice crocheters have transformed a village church with a cascade of woollen memorial poppies.

Caroline Moore and Wendy Ireland took up their crochet hooks last November with the aim of creating a display for their village of Friston in Suffolk.

The pair said they came up with the idea after "a few glasses of wine" after being inspired by a display on Southend Pier in Essex last November which they saw on social media.

"Many hours of love and thought have gone into this," said Ireland.

"This has been a year in the making but this is our first time - so we're novices and we've only just learnt to crochet," she added.

Moore said they decided to invite other people in the village which led to a group of women joining for a "knit and natter" over a cup of tea and cake.

The exact number of poppies on the installation is being kept secret, so as not to spoil a competition for people to guess the total.

However, the pair said the amount meant they had slashed their poppy making time from an hour to just 20 minutes per poppy thanks to all the practice.

articles.title: How computer game Worms went from classroom to classic
articles.summary: Creator Andy Davidson speaks to the BBC about how he created a game that sold 70 million copies.
articles.body:
Andy Davidson was 22 when the game he programmed, partly in his last years at Bournemouth School, first hit the shelves.

Thirty-one years later, the various incarnations of Worms have sold enough copies that everyone in the UK could have one.

Davidson said: "Across all formats and all versions of the game it's up to 70 million now. I just can't get my head around it."

Worms is a turn-based artillery game where players control a team of invertebrates who use a variety of creative ways to destroy their opponents.

Options included dynamite, homing missile, or exploding sheep.

Davidson said: "I chose worms because they hadn't been in a game before.

"I thought I could get a lot of character into the animations because they're quite simple creatures."

In fact, the game itself had very simple beginnings.

Bored during his A-levels, Davidson started programming an early incarnation of the game into his scientific calculator.

"I found A-levels really hard, especially maths," he said.

"So I challenged my friend to make a game on a calculator. It was a little Casio graph-plotting calculator.

"And if you really pushed it hard you could get it to make a game. And so I made this little tank game. It snowballed from there."

Davidson's art teacher at the time was John Pakeman.

Pakeman was intrigued by what computers like Davidson's Amiga could do when it came to art.

"Once I saw what it was capable of I thought perhaps I better get one of these," he said.

"There was so much interest from other sixth formers in the school that it was almost inevitable a club would come together."

It was partly in Pakeman's Amiga club that the game, which was originally called Total Wormage, started to take shape.

"The game got banned from school," said Davidson.

"Everyone was crowding around the corner in the art room. That's when I thought I might be onto something."

Even though he was there at the time, Pakeman was not sure of the potential impact of the game.

"I wasn't sure if Andy created something, whether he could find a company that would take it on," said Pakeman.

"I gather that's exactly what happened, he did find one, eventually.

"I have never played the game. I think I've screenshots of it and I have friends who definitely have played the game.

"You mention Worms and they start beaming. My research tells me it's quite addictive."

Davidson signed with the West Yorkshire based company Team 17 to release Worms in November 1995.

Its legacy is impressive - it was one of six British games celebrated on a special series of stamps in January 2020.

"When worms was on a stamp that's when it really hit home for my mum - she was telling everybody it's been on a Royal Mail stamp."

And Davidson's teenage voice still lives on in many people's mobile phones.

"I did the voices of all the angry worms," he said.

"I think 'Incoming' is the most famous one because people use it for text messages on their phones.

"It's bonkers. In my head it's still the little game I made for me and my friends."

articles.title: Nepal’s fight to rebuild after flood disaster
articles.summary: 101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a devastating natural disaster.
articles.body:
On the morning of August 26, 2026, a devastating flash flood of rock and ice thundered from a high Himalayan mountain through Nepal’s valleys, sweeping away homes, villages and bridges.

At least 1,400 people were killed and more than 5,000 people remain missing.

It was the latest in a series of natural disasters that have battered Nepal in recent years as climate change accelerates.

This programme follows the rescuers risking their lives to search for the missing and those providing aid and refuge for traumatised children and families.

101 East reveals Nepal’s efforts to save lives and rebuild communities after a deadly natural disaster.

articles.title: Ataques da Rússia na Ucrânia: Kiev fica sem luz e aquecimento | G1
articles.standfirst: Pelo menos duas pessoas morreram e cerca de uma dúzia ficaram feridas após 36 mísseis balísticos e 172 drones serem lançados contra o território ucraniano.
articles.summary: Pelo menos duas pessoas morreram e cerca de uma dúzia ficaram feridas após 36 mísseis balísticos e 172 drones serem lançados contra o território ucraniano.
articles.body:
Bombeiros trabalham no local de um ataque com míssil russo em Kiev — Foto: REUTERS/Gleb Garanich

A Rússia bombardeou a infraestrutura energética da Ucrânia com mísseis e drones durante a madrugada deste sábado (7), danificando e sobrecarregando o fornecimento de energia e os sistemas de aquecimento de Kiev , enquanto as temperaturas se aproximavam dos 0ºC , segundo autoridades ucranianas.

De acordo com o presidente Volodymyr Zelensky , 36 mísseis balísticos e 172 drones - dos quais 149 foram abatidos pela Força Aérea do país - foram lançados contra o território ucraniano, principalmente contra instalações de energia.

"A capital enfrenta sérias dificuldades com o fornecimento de eletricidade, água e aquecimento", disse Zelensky em post na rede social X, acrescentando que subestações da capital, Kiev, e outras cinco regiões foram afetadas.

Um dos ataques também atingiu e danificou uma importante ponte, a Ponte Norte sobre o rio Dnipro , de acordo com o prefeito de Kiev, Vitali Klitschko.

Pelo menos duas pessoas morreram e cerca de uma dúzia ficaram feridas . Casas, empresas e edifícios não residenciais também foram danificados, disseram as autoridades.

Morador de apartamento atingido é fotografado agasalhado por causa das baixas temperaturas e falta de aquecimento — Foto: REUTERS/Gleb Garanich

O Ministério da Defesa de Moscou confirmou ter realizado um ataque massivo contra alvos que descreveu como pertencentes ao setor militar-industrial da Ucrânia , bem como à infraestrutura de energia e transporte em Kiev e arredores.

Os ataques ocorrem dias antes de uma nova rodada de negociações tripartidas em Abu Dhabi entre autoridades ucranianas e russas , como parte de uma iniciativa de paz apoiada pelos EUA que até agora produziu poucos resultados.

"A Rússia está se preparando para negociações trilaterais lançando mísseis balísticos contra a infraestrutura crítica da Ucrânia ", criticou Zelensky no X.

Um vídeo divulgado pela Polícia Nacional da Ucrânia nesta quinta-feira (5) mostrou o momento em que um bombardeio russo atingiu uma escola que servia para distribuição de ajuda humanitária em Zaporizhzhia.

Segundo balanço, 43 pessoas morreram no ataque.

O ataque aéreo ocorreu na segunda-feira (2), e Zelensky acusou a Rússia de realizar um bombardeio duplo —conhecido como "double tap", em inglês—, que é proibido pela Convenção de Genebra. Equipes de resgate continuam nesta quinta-feira as buscas por dezenas de pessoas que estão desaparecidas.

O vídeo mostra equipes de segurança e civis do lado de fora do complexo subterrâneo —que funcionava como uma escola antes da guerra e foi adaptado para distribuição de suprimentos—, e em dado momento, após receber alerta de ataque aéreo, eles todos descem escadas e vão para uma sala. Então, o ataque atinge o local e destrói o complexo. Veja no vídeo acima.

Equipes de resgate buscam vítimas de ataque aéreo russo em escola subterrânea que servia como centro de distribuição humanitária em Zaporizhzhia, na Ucrânia, em 4 de novembro de 2026. — Foto: REUTERS/Sergiy Chalyi

O presidente ucraniano, Volodymyr Zelensky, repudiou os ataques em suas redes sociais e também em um pronunciamento em vídeo. De acordo com Zelensky, a região teria sido atingida várias vezes por bombas aéreas.

"Os ataques tiveram como alvo uma escola utilizada para fins humanitários: era lá que as pessoas recebiam ajuda humanitária. Após o primeiro bombardeio, houve um segundo ataque, com mais nove bombas, que atingiu especificamente o abrigo onde as pessoas haviam buscado proteção", afirmou.

➡️ Um bombardeio duplo, como acusado por Zelensky, é conhecido como "double tap" e costuma ser usada para atingir equipes de socorro, jornalistas e civis em geral, os quais não são considerados alvos legítimos pelo direito internacional. Essa prática pode ser considerada crime de guerra nos termos da Terceira Convenção de Genebra, de 1949.

articles.title: Cratera avança e se aproxima de cemitério no interior do Acre | G1
articles.standfirst: Outros pontos de Rodrigues Alves, como a região do porto, também registram desbarrancamento. O município busca recursos federais e estaduais para obras de contenção.
articles.summary: Outros pontos de Rodrigues Alves, como a região do porto, também registram desbarrancamento. O município busca recursos federais e estaduais para obras de contenção.
articles.body:
Município de Rodrigues Alves registra outros pontos de desbarrancamento — Foto: Defesa Civil

Autoridades de Rodrigues Alves , no interior do Acre, monitoram o avanço de erosão no solo próximo ao Cemitério Municipal. Imagens registradas durante vistorias mostram uma cratera se aproximando do muro do espaço.

O local foi incluído no decreto de emergência publicado pelo Governo do Acre nessa quinta-feira (5) , junto ao calçadão do Novo Mercado Velho, em Rio Branco . Os dois locais são apontados como risco geológico.

Segundo o coordenador da Defesa Civil de Rodrigues Alves, José Adgarbe Pereira Alves, além do cemitério, outros pontos do município também apresentam problemas relacionados ao desbarrancamento. A situação levou o município a buscar apoio técnico da Defesa Civil Estadual para avaliar as condições.

"A Prefeitura de Rodrigues Alves já está buscando providências diante da situação de desbarrancamento registrada na área do cemitério municipal, que apresenta riscos e exige atenção especial do poder público", disse.

A região do porto da cidade também preocupa, já que a movimentação de solo registrada no local compromete trechos de vias e estruturas utilizadas pela população. A prefeitura solicitou um estudo técnico para avaliar a gravidade da situação e identificar os riscos existentes.

A preocupação segundo Alves, é evitar que o avanço da erosão comprometa ainda mais a estrutura do local. O município busca o reconhecimento da situação de emergência para viabilizar apoio dos governos estadual e federal e conseguir recursos destinados a obras de contenção e recuperação.

As autoridades anunciaram ainda, além do decreto, notificação formal da empresa contratada responsável pelas obras, a retirada temporária de feirantes da economia solidária e a elaboração de um plano de remanejamento para os permissionários afetados.

Técnicos do estado e da gestão da capital fizeram uma vistoria conjunta no calçadão. A governadora Mailza Assis (PP) e o prefeito de Rio Branco, Alysson Bestene (PP), também concederam entrevista coletiva para falar das medidas para solucionar a degradação do local.

"Já está sendo feito um monitoramento diário sobre as condições da obra e, agora, chegamos à conclusão de que é necessária a publicação de um decreto para a retirada de parte dos comerciantes do trecho que oferece risco, evitando qualquer fatalidade”, afirmou a governadora.

articles.title: Árvore Solidária 2026 da TV TEM: veja como doar brinquedos na campanha | G1
articles.standfirst: Em sua quarta edição, a iniciativa, promovida pela emissora, destinará as doações a famílias e crianças em estado de vulnerabilidade social.
articles.summary: A Árvore Solidária 2026 arrecada brinquedos novos e usados em Sorocaba, Bauru e outras cidades até 12 de dezembro; confira os pontos de coleta e participe.
articles.body:
A TV TEM realiza a partir deste sábado (7) a quarta edição da campanha Árvore Solidária, que arrecada brinquedos novos e usados em bom estado. A ação será realizada até o dia 12 de dezembro em Itapetininga, Sorocaba , Jundiaí , Bauru , Marília e São José do Rio Preto (SP).

A iniciativa, promovida pela emissora, destinará as doações a famílias e crianças em estado de vulnerabilidade social. No dia 12 de dezembro será realizado o "Dia D" , que funciona como a última chamada para as doações.

Campanha Árvore Solidária da TV TEM está na quarta edição e arrecada brinquedos em cidades do interior paulista — Foto: Kauã Bueno/g1

Toda a comunidade é convidada a participar. As doações devem ser entregues nos pontos de coleta dos parceiros comerciais ( veja abaixo ) ou na recepção das emissoras participantes, em dias úteis e durante o horário comercial, em Sorocaba, Bauru, São José do Rio Preto e Itapetininga (SP).

Para que o movimento se concretize, o projeto conta com o apoio dos Correios para triagem, contagem e destinação das doações. A entrega será no dia 14 de dezembro.

Sedes da emissora também serão locais de arrecadação dos brinquedos na campanha Árvore Solidária — Foto: Kauã Bueno / g1

Os parceiros desta edição são: Anauger e USCS em Itapetininga; Proença em São José do Rio Preto; Tauste, em Bauru; e Tauste, em Sorocaba .

As entidades beneficiadas são selecionadas através de uma triagem conduzida pela TV TEM em conjunto com apoiadores, que destina as doações a instituições assistenciais locais e a outras campanhas de Natal de seus apoiadores.

Na edição de 2025, centenas de crianças em situação de vulnerabilidade foram contempladas por instituições como Apae Rio Preto; Casa Thales, Associação Amor de Mãe, em Marília; Associação Acolhimento Bom Pastor, em Jundiaí; Sexta é Nóis, em Itapetininga, e Projeto Red Tails, em Sorocaba.

Cerca de 60 mil brinquedos já foram arrecadados nas edições anteriores.

articles.title: Enem em Manaus: Prefeitura anuncia ônibus gratuito nos dias de prova | G1
articles.standfirst: Gratuidade valerá neste domingo (8) e no dia 15 de novembro, das 7h às 20h, nos ônibus convencionais do transporte coletivo. Candidatos deverão apresentar o cartão de inscrição e um documento oficial com foto.
articles.summary: Candidatos do Enem em Manaus terão ônibus gratuito nos dias 8 e 15 de novembro, das 7h às 20h, mediante apresentação do cartão de inscrição e documento oficial.
articles.body:
Linhas de ônibus que atendem em Manaus — Foto: Divulgação/IMMU

A Prefeitura de Manaus anunciou, neste sábado (7), que os candidatos que farão o Exame Nacional do Ensino Médio (Enem) terão direito a transporte gratuito nos ônibus convencionais da capital nos dois dias de aplicação das provas.

Segundo o prefeito de Manaus, Renato Junior, a gratuidade será oferecida neste domingo (8) e no próximo dia 15 de novembro, das 7h às 20h.

Para utilizar o benefício, o candidato deverá apresentar o cartão de inscrição do Enem e um documento oficial com foto ao entrar no ônibus. A medida não vale para os veículos alternativos, conhecidos como “amarelinhos”.

Em publicação nas redes sociais, o prefeito afirmou que esta é a primeira vez que a prefeitura custeará as passagens dos candidatos durante os dias de aplicação do exame.

“Eu sei que, para muitos jovens, o Enem representa a oportunidade de entrar numa universidade, conquistar uma profissão e mudar não apenas a própria vida, mas a história de uma família inteira. E não é uma passagem de ônibus que pode ser empecilho ou barreira para quem está lutando para ter um futuro melhor”, disse.

As provas do Enem serão aplicadas em dois domingos, nos dias 8 e 15 de novembro.

No primeiro dia, os candidatos responderão às questões de Linguagens, Códigos e suas Tecnologias e Ciências Humanas e suas Tecnologias, além de fazerem a redação. O encerramento está previsto para as 18h, no horário local.

No segundo domingo, serão aplicadas as provas de Matemática e suas Tecnologias e Ciências da Natureza e suas Tecnologias, com término previsto para as 17h30.

Em Manaus, os portões dos locais de aplicação serão abertos às 11h e fechados pontualmente ao meio-dia. As provas têm início previsto para as 12h30.

A orientação é que os candidatos planejem o trajeto com antecedência e fiquem atentos ao horário de fechamento dos portões.

Mais de 41 mil alunos da rede estadual de ensino, na capital e no interior do Amazonas, estão inscritos para realizar o exame neste ano.

articles.title: Obra no antigo Colégio Bennett provoca rachaduras em prédios vizinhos | G1
articles.standfirst: Defesa Civil relacionou os danos à construção no terreno do antigo Colégio Bennett, mas não identificou risco iminente à estrutura. Estudantes e moradores relatam problemas.
articles.summary: Defesa Civil relacionou os danos à construção no terreno do antigo Colégio Bennett, mas não identificou risco iminente à estrutura. Estudantes e moradores relatam problemas.
articles.body:
Rachaduras profundas apareceram em diferentes pontos de prédios vizinhos a uma obra de construção de um condomínio no terreno do antigo Colégio Bennett , no Flamengo, na Zona Sul do Rio. Os problemas foram identificados na faculdade Uninassau e em imóveis residenciais do entorno.

Após uma vistoria, a Defesa Civil confirmou que os danos estão relacionados à obra , mas não identificou risco iminente à estrutura.

Na faculdade, estudantes registraram fissuras na biblioteca, nos banheiros e nos corredores . Eles relatam preocupação com as condições do prédio e também reclamam do barulho provocado pela construção, inclusive durante as aulas noturnas.

Obra no antigo Colégio Bennett provoca rachaduras em prédios vizinhos no Flamengo — Foto: Reprodução TV Globo

A suspeita dos alunos é que as rachaduras tenham sido provocadas pela movimentação da obra, que ocupa o terreno onde funcionava o antigo colégio.

A reitoria da Uninassau informou que engenheiros especializados fizeram uma vistoria no imóvel e não identificaram indícios de comprometimento estrutural que justificassem a suspensão das aulas.

A Defesa Civil fez uma vistoria no prédio da faculdade e confirmou que os danos identificados estão relacionados à construção vizinha. Apesar das trincas e rachaduras, os técnicos não encontraram risco iminente à estrutura.

Segundo as informações da vistoria, a construtora responsável já iniciou o acompanhamento dos danos. A Secretaria Municipal de Desenvolvimento Urbano e Licenciamento também foi acionada para fiscalizar a obra.

Os problemas também atingiram imóveis residenciais próximos ao canteiro de obras.

Uma moradora, a engenheira Gabriella Zullo, relatou que as primeiras rachaduras e o descolamento de partes da estrutura de seu apartamento começaram em outubro , na área de serviço. Nesta semana, uma pedra de tamanho considerável caiu de uma parte do prédio.

Outro caso preocupa o síndico Marcelo Silva. Um sobrado que antes ficava encostado ao edifício vizinho à obra agora apresenta um afastamento entre as estruturas. A abertura já tem aproximadamente a largura de um dedo.

O condomínio solicitou uma vistoria da Defesa Civil, prevista para o dia 16.

Em nota, a empresa New View Incorporadora, responsável pelo empreendimento, afirmou que as fissuras identificadas nos imóveis vizinhos são superficiais e que não há qualquer dano estrutural.

A incorporadora disse ainda que está monitorando os outros prédios do entorno, mantém diálogo com os moradores e que vai realizar os reparos necessários.

Obra já foi alvo de mobilização de moradores

A construção no terreno do antigo Colégio Bennett já havia provocado mobilização de moradores do Flamengo. Eles se organizaram contra a retirada de cerca de 70 árvores centenárias existentes na área, onde funcionou a antiga residência do Barão de São Clemente.

Em janeiro de 2026, a Justiça determinou a suspensão imediata das obras do empreendimento imobiliário . A decisão ocorreu após moradores entrarem com uma ação questionando a derrubada das árvores em um terreno tombado pelo município.

Agora, com o surgimento de rachaduras na faculdade e os danos relatados por moradores de imóveis vizinhos, a obra voltou a provocar preocupação na região.

articles.title: A couple claimed every dollar would save starving babies in Malawi; the charity founders diverted more than $2 million for cosmetic surgery, cruises and luxury holidays
articles.summary: Donors who supported an Arkansas charity were told their contributions would help feed and protect vulnerable babies in Malawi, one of the world's poorest
articles.body: Donors who supported an Arkansas charity were told their contributions would help feed and protect vulnerable babies in Malawi, one of the world's poorest countries. The organisation, called 2nd Milk, presented itself as a ministry where sponsorship money went towards children rather than the personal expenses of its founders. But an investigation into its finances uncovered a different use for the donations. According to the US Department of Justice, more than $2 million was diverted to cover expenses ranging from cosmetic surgery and massages to international holidays, cruises and household bills. The charity's founders, Jason Boyd Carney and his wife, Lacey Christina Carney, have now been sentenced to prison after their involvement in the scheme was established in federal court.Arkansas charity founders receive maximum prison sentences for $2 million fraudThe couple, who founded 2nd Milk in Springdale, Arkansas, were sentenced on October 14, 2026, in the Western District of Arkansas. Jason Carney received 192 months in federal prison, equivalent to 16 years, for offences connected to conspiracy, wire fraud and tax fraud. He will also serve three years of supervised release after completing his prison term.His wife, Lacey Carney, received a 36-month prison sentence for failing to report her husband's fraudulent activities despite knowing about the scheme. Her sentence also includes one year of supervised release. Federal prosecutors said both punishments represented the maximum prison terms permitted under the counts for which they were convicted.Reportedly, Chief US District Judge Timothy L. Brooks presided over the sentencing. In describing Jason Carney's actions, the judge used the words "profoundly disgusting", calling the conduct "egregious, repulsive, and violative". The sentences followed an investigation involving Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation and the Diplomatic Security Service.How 2nd Milk founders convinced donors their money was helping starving babiesFor several years, Jason Carney presented 2nd Milk as an organisation with a clear financial commitment to the children it supported. Its fundraising messages placed particular emphasis on transparency, with donors encouraged to believe that sponsorship contributions were being used for their intended purpose.The promises were unusually direct. Carney told potential supporters that all sponsorship money went towards saving vulnerable babies in developing countries. In another assurance, he said that 82 cents of every dollar went to babies, while the remainder covered overhead expenses in Africa. He also maintained that neither he nor his wife took money from people sponsoring children.Carney repeatedly insisted that he had never received a salary from the organisation. One of his assurances stated that all the money went specifically towards the children. Prosecutors later presented these statements as part of the evidence showing how donors had been persuaded to continue supporting the charity.The organisation's stated purpose was to help orphaned and malnourished children in Malawi. Supporters were therefore contributing on the understanding that their money would provide assistance to a particularly vulnerable group, rather than finance the personal lives of those running the organisation.Charity money paid for cosmetic procedures, cruises and overseas holidaysThe financial investigation uncovered payments that prosecutors said had little connection to 2nd Milk's charitable work. Bank records showed that money belonging to the nonprofit had been used to meet a range of personal expenses for Jason and Lacey Carney.Among the purchases and payments identified were cosmetic surgery, massages, tanning services and expenses involving their pets. Charity funds also went towards a cruise, mortgage payments on the couple's home, and loans connected to their cars and boat. Investigators also traced money used for luxury travel.The couple visited several international destinations, including Rome, Chile, Peru, Japan, Barcelona, Cancun and Vietnam. These trips were among the personal expenses that prosecutors linked to the diversion of charitable contributions.The misuse of donations was accompanied by efforts to conceal the financial activity. Prosecutors established that Jason Carney submitted false tax returns for himself and 2nd Milk, including an inaccurate annual nonprofit return, to hide the diversion of funds.Jason Carney admitted fraud and tax offences during his trialThe criminal proceedings included a jury trial, although Jason Carney changed his position before the prosecution had completed presenting its case. On the sixth day of the trial, he entered guilty pleas to four counts.These included conspiracy to commit wire fraud, two counts of filing false tax returns and one count of structuring cash transactions to avoid reporting requirements. The tax offences covered his personal return and the charity's Form 990, which nonprofits use to report financial and organisational information to the Internal Revenue Service.The structuring charge concerned the handling of cash transactions in a way intended to evade the reporting requirements that apply to certain financial activity. Together, the offences formed part of the case against him over the use of charity money and the concealment of its movement.Lacey Carney, aged 47, pleaded guilty to one count of misprision of a felony. The offence relates to knowing that a federal crime has been committed and deliberately failing to report it to the appropriate authorities. Prosecutors said she knew about her husband's wire fraud scheme but did not disclose it as required by law. Jason Carney was 48 at the time of the proceedings. Both defendants were held responsible for their respective offences, although the charges and sentences against them were different.Couple agreed to give up their homeThe financial consequences of the case also extended to the couple's property. Jason and Lacey Carney agreed to forfeit their home after authorities established that proceeds from the wire fraud had been used towards mortgage payments.The forfeiture formed part of the financial penalties connected to the criminal proceedings. It also reflected the extent to which money diverted from 2nd Milk had been used to support the couple's personal assets and living expenses.The case was announced by the US Attorney's Office for the Western District of Arkansas as part of a wider federal enforcement effort targeting fraud and tax-related offences. The Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division and IRS Criminal Investigation were among the agencies involved in the nationwide initiative.Federal officials respond to misuse of charitable donationsUS Attorney Kevin R. Holmes said the sentences demonstrated the consequences for people who use charitable organisations to obtain personal financial benefits. He said the Carneys had violated the confidence placed in them by donors whose contributions were intended to support vulnerable children.IRS Criminal Investigation Special Agent in Charge Donald "Trey" Eakins also addressed the case, pointing to the difference between what donors believed they were funding and how the money was actually spent. He said contributions intended to help malnourished and orphaned infants had instead been diverted towards personal expenses.Nicholas Collura, principal deputy assistant secretary for diplomatic security and director of the Diplomatic Security Service, said the case illustrated the damage caused when charitable causes are used for personal gain. The agency had worked with federal investigators to uncover the financial activity.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Democratic rights were curtailed but constitutionally': Sonia Gandhi reflects on Emergency
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP) Chairperson Sonia Gandhi has accused the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government of causing significant
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress Parliamentary Party (CPP) Chairperson Sonia Gandhi has accused the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) government of causing significant damage to India's democratic institutions over the past 12 years, expressing confidence that the country's electorate would eventually bring about a return to proper governance.In an interview with The Hindu, Sonia said the damage extended to the country's democratic fabric and institutions, adding that people were increasingly recognising the consequences of the government's actions."Over the last twelve years, great damage has been done to the fabric of our country, our democracy and our institutions," she said.She expressed optimism about the country's political future, while acknowledging that restoring democratic institutions and governance would require considerable time and effort, even after the present government leaves office."Even after this government goes, it will take time to restore our systems to health, and great effort from political parties. People are now beginning to be restless and recognising the damage. But I am optimistic, and I know that the people of India will welcome a return to proper governance," she said.Sonia Gandhi on the 1975 EmergencyReflecting on the 1975 Emergency imposed by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, Sonia Gandhi acknowledged that democratic rights had been curtailed during the 21-month period but said the decision was taken constitutionally."It was only after the Emergency that I came to know the true gravity of what had been happening. Yes, democratic rights had been curtailed, and there was a suspension of habeas corpus, but it was done constitutionally," she said.She also offered her perspective on the circumstances leading to the imposition of the Emergency, referring to violent protests, attacks on government offices and public transport, widespread unrest and calls for the bureaucracy and armed forces to disobey orders.Also read: Court allows more evidence in Sonia Gandhi voter list case"Yet, when I take myself back to that period and try and see it from Mrs Gandhi's (Indira Gandhi) point of view, I see her struggling to cope with the rapidly deteriorating prevailing circumstances: violent protests, government offices and public transport set on fire, widespread organised unrest and even a call for the bureaucracy and armed forces to disobey orders," she said.Sonia further noted that Indira Gandhi eventually recognised the situation, called for general elections in March 1977 and later publicly acknowledged and apologised for the excesses committed during the Emergency."Hindsight allows us to put things better in perspective. Let's not forget that it was Mrs Gandhi herself who came to recognise what was happening and called for the March 1977 election. And you know very well that she herself later publicly expressed regret and apologised for excesses during the Emergency," she said.Meanwhile, the BJP hit back at Sonia Gandhi over her criticism of the central government, with Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal invoking the 1975 Emergency and questioning her remarks on democracy.Speaking to reporters in Bikaner, Rajasthan, Meghwal said Gandhi should also recall the period when democratic rights were curtailed, opposition leaders were jailed and journalists were silenced."The article makes certain observations regarding democracy. I would like to ask Sonia ji: does she not recall the period of 1975, when democracy was strangled? Thousands of senior leaders from various political parties were thrown into jail, and the voices of journalists were silenced. She ought to remember that era as well. In contrast, over the last 12 years, PM Modi has nurtured, flourished, and strengthened democracy, proclaiming to the entire world that India is the 'mother of democracy.' It is Prime Minister Narendra Modi who has emphatically declared that 'India is the mother of democracy,'" he said.Responding to the opposition's demand for a special parliamentary session, Meghwal said the government was ready for a debate and urged opposition parties to submit a proposal. He also referred to the Home Minister's remarks at a rally in Haryana, saying Parliament was the appropriate forum for such discussions."Our Home Minister provided a fitting response (to Rahul Gandhi) at a rally in Haryana, pointing out that the Constitution-makers designated Parliament as the proper venue for such debates. If the opposition wishes to engage in a discussion, let them put forward a proposal; we can certainly convene a special session—there is no issue with that. The Prime Minister has also expressed a similar sentiment. As for the suggestion that someone should act as a 'judge'—our democratic system already has a mechanism for this; the Speaker serves as the arbiter. What is new about this proposal? Why not simply debate? Who is stopping them? They have written requesting a special session; the government is prepared to call one. We are ready for a debate," he said.Reacting to Sonia’s article, Union Minister Giriraj Singh launched a sharp attack on her, questioning her remarks on democracy and making allegations about her and her son’s citizenship."Sonia Gandhi, may God grant you a long life. You have grown weary from trying to 'launch' your son. You speak of democracy? You should be ashamed... You lived in this country for 12 years without citizenship, and it is alleged that you even cast a vote. Questions are also being raised regarding your son's citizenship. Abandon these ambitions. Forget about a return in 10 years; the Congress will never return to power in this country. You haven't held power in nine different states for the last 40 years. Sonia Gandhi, from the very Congress party that imposed the Emergency and silenced the voices of the people, is talking about democracy. You and your son are trying to incite a civil war in India; that ambition, too, will never be fulfilled."Sonia Gandhi's memoir 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'The Congress leader also spoke about her upcoming memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, describing it as an account of how she grew to love her husband and former Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi's family and India, and how that connection eventually brought her into public life.In the interview, she said she had long been reluctant to share her personal story but eventually decided to write about the experiences that shaped her life and her decision to enter politics."I had no desire to talk about it for so long. But it is not only a love story between the two of us, but it's also the story of how I grew to love Rajiv's family and the country to which they belonged, and then I too came to belong in it. And of how this love brought me into public life, when I saw the purpose of all the sacrifices they had made being threatened, and the party was weakening. I felt I had to do something," she said.The memoir traces Sonia's journey from her childhood in post-war Italy and her romance with Rajiv Gandhi, which brought her to India, to the personal losses that shaped her life and her relationship with her adopted country. It also recounts her experiences as a member of the Nehru-Gandhi family and her journey from private life to public service.The book, her first memoir, is scheduled to be launched on November 10.Rahul Gandhi expresses pride over mother's memoirEarlier, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi had expressed his excitement over the publication of his mother's memoir, saying he was proud that her personal story would reach readers.On the 82nd birth anniversary of his father, Rajiv Gandhi, Rahul said he understood how difficult it had been for his mother, who preferred to maintain a private life, to share her experiences publicly."I am happy, and so proud, that your story--'Belonging: A Journey of Love'--will finally be read by the millions of people who love you. I know how hard it was for someone as private as you to tell the world your beautiful story. Today, on his birthday, I can see Papa smiling and looking down proudly at his beautiful Sonia," Rahul Gandhi said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Netanyahu planned Iran attack before Israel polls; operative's mistaken tip to US stopped it: Report
articles.summary: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad chief Roman Gofman reportedly sought to launch an operation against Iran just before Israel's October
articles.body: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad chief Roman Gofman reportedly sought to launch an operation against Iran just before Israel's October 27 election, but the plan was stopped after the United States was alerted.The proposed operation was said to be opposed by senior officials in Israel's security establishment. They feared it could trigger a major escalation with Iran and disrupt the election. Despite these concerns, preparations for the unspecified operation continued. However, a mistake by an Israeli security operative reportedly tipped off Washington about the plan. The US then moved quickly to prevent the operation from going ahead, Channel 12 reported, as quoted by Times of Israel.Netanyahu's office rejected the report, saying: “The prime minister himself clarified in real time that an attack before the Israeli elections was not on the agenda.”The latest report follows a series of accounts in Israeli media about tensions between Netanyahu and senior military officials over possible action against Iran in the run-up to the election.Also read: Iran rebuilding missile sites, moving military infrastructure underground to evade strikesOn October 25, Channel 12 reported an “unprecedented confrontation” between Netanyahu and Israel Defence Forces (IDF) Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir over an order for unspecified military action. According to that report, Zamir resisted carrying out the instruction, sought further deliberations and asked Netanyahu to provide written authorisation for the move.Military officials were concerned that the proposed action could trigger a wider confrontation with Iran at a sensitive moment. The report also cited concerns that the political leadership could be seeking to use the Iran issue for electoral advantage.Netanyahu dismissed the account as “nonsense” in an interview with Channel 14, saying there had been “no fight” with Zamir. He had separately said he had instructed the IDF and Mossad to topple the Iranian regime.A day later, Channels 12 and 13 reported that Zamir was the only senior Israeli security chief opposing military action sought by Netanyahu and Defence Minister Israel Katz, amid fears it could escalate tensions with Iran and derail the election.Also read: 'Israel, Middle East wouldn't exist today': Trump boasts of stopping Iran's nuclear ambitionsIran talks complicate Netanyahu's push for strikesThe reported attempt to launch an operation comes amid diplomatic efforts to end the conflict between the US and Iran, with Qatar mediating negotiations. US President Donald Trump has indicated that he wants to give diplomacy more time, even as the possibility of renewed military action remains.Channel 12 reported earlier this week that Netanyahu had urged Trump to resume the war against Iran immediately after the US midterm elections. Trump, however, reportedly wanted Israel to avoid disrupting negotiations with Tehran.Netanyahu is said to be concerned that a diplomatic agreement could lead to a significant easing of pressure on Iran.Asked about Iran outside the White House on Friday, Trump said, “We've beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran. We're talking to Iran. We haven't lost a soldier in six or seven months.”He also repeated his claim that Israel and the wider Middle East would not exist today had he not stopped Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.The latest Channel 12 report marks a second alleged instance in which Washington intervened to prevent Israeli military action against Iran. The Financial Times had earlier reported that Trump opposed a separate Israeli plan for a more extensive offensive, which was reportedly ready to be launched on October 10.You use AI every day. articles.title: Children's pain after learning mum Patricia Lashley was killed by Trevor Dunkley
articles.summary: The children of Patricia Lashley grew up believing their mother had abandoned them.
articles.body:
The children of a woman who was murdered 28 years ago have spoken of their anger after growing up believing their mother had abandoned them.

Patricia Lashley, 33, a mother of seven, was last seen near her home in Hall Street, Dudley, in September 1998.

Her partner Trevor Dunkley, now 66, was jailed for life , with a minimum term of 10 years and 10 months, at Wolverhampton Crown Court on Friday, after admitting her murder earlier this year. Lashley's remains have never been found.

After the sentencing, her eldest son Sinan Mehmet said he and his siblings had believed their mother had abandoned them, leaving them feeling resentful. "We always felt like we were unwanted," he said.

"We didn't have anyone to support us really in our lives. We struggled growing up," added Mehmet.

They were unaware that their mother had been beaten to death by her partner before hiding her body in the cellar of their home for about a year before disposing of her remains in household waste bins.

The court heard Dunkley had maintained his account that Lashley had disappeared for decades, despite being spoken to by police multiple times.

He said she had left her youngest child, who was not Dunkley's son, alone in their flat. Dunkley took the nine-month-old to social services and he was later adopted.

Judge Chambers said the "most significant aggravating factor" in the case was that Dunkley had killed the mother of a baby, who she had still been breastfeeding.

Mehmet said Dunkley killed his mother "in such a horrible way and then lied to us for 27 years", and that learning about her death had made him feel guilty about the resentment he had felt in the past.

"I feel bad in a way now that I felt that way towards mum," he said.

Mehmet said the past few months had been among the hardest of his life as the family had been forced to confront what happened to their mother and hear details of her killing.

Dunkley confessed to the murder in July after a police officer "pointed out... the impact on the family". He became emotional and told police: "I killed her, I'm sorry."

Mehmet said he felt anger towards Dunkley: "I don't have any gratitude towards him even though he thinks he's done the right thing by coming forward."

His sister, Destine, said she felt "mixed emotions". She said she and her siblings had been left in foster homes and children's homes after their mother's disappearance.

She said she could not forgive Dunkley, who "could have rung the police at the time".

The judge said Dunkley's confession was "to his credit" but the delay in bringing the case to justice had been caused by his lies.

"You did a dreadful thing and the passage of time is only down to your untruths," he told him.

Dunkley also received a concurrent two-year sentence for preventing Lashley's lawful burial.

articles.title: New Zealand election first count ends with two main parties nearly deadlocked
articles.summary: New Zealand’s ruling centre-right National Party and main opposition Labour were near deadlocked in the ​popular vote as counting began in the nationwide general election on Saturday.
articles.body: WELLINGTON — New Zealand’s ruling centre-right National Party and main opposition ​Labour were nearly deadlocked in the popular vote after initial counting in the nationwide general election on Saturday. Results from the Electoral Commission ‌show that with more than 95% of the ballots counted, both parties were polling just short of 30% of the popular vote, with just a few thousand votes separating the two. A projection from New Zealand’s ​Electoral Commission showed the current three-party ruling coalition led by National would have a ​majority of just one seat, after an election dominated by a struggling economy ⁠and voter disillusionment with the two biggest contenders. Both parties said it would take time for the final results to be known. “It is heartening to see that ​on the numbers so far, National is once again the largest party in parliament, and we have a pathway to forming ⁠the next government,” Prime Minister Christopher Luxon told supporters in Auckland. “But I have to tell you right now, it is too close to call.” Labour leader Chris ​Hipkins delivered a similar message in Upper Hutt, a city northeast of the capital Wellington. “Tonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to ​figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said,” he told supporters. Special votes, which include those from overseas voters or people outside their electorate, will not be included in the vote count until official results are released on November 27. Those votes have typically favoured the left, with parties on the right losing support following the count. This could also ​be key in seats where races remain tight between Labour and National candidates. Left-leaning parties including Labour are aiming to make the National-led coalition the first one-term government ​in just over 50 years. New Zealand’s electoral system makes coalitions the norm, and the tightness of this year’s race means one or more of the country’s smaller parties will almost ‌certainly participate ⁠in a governing coalition. The country switched to a mixed member proportional system in 1996, which means people vote for both the party and a local constituency candidate. There are 71 constituency seats and at least 49 party seats, and a party or coalition needs a majority to form a government. Popular support for Labour and National is at historically low levels, with surveys showing voters have lost faith in the major parties to find solutions to the sluggish economy and to ​make the necessary changes to fix ​ageing infrastructure. If the National-led coalition loses ⁠its majority at the official count, either it or a left-leaning coalition would require the support of the centrist Opportunity Party, which looks likely to enter parliament for the first time. Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong said she would look to negotiate with ​the party that secured the largest number of seats after the official results. “We made that call based on the fact ​that we need a ⁠majority of seats in parliament in order to form a government. So that is what we will stick to,” she told public broadcaster TVNZ. New Zealand has emerged only slowly from a prolonged economic downturn, with growth subdued, household budgets strained and unemployment rising to 5.7% in the third quarter, its highest level in 11 years. Healthcare and hospitals ⁠rank alongside the ​economy as leading concerns for voters, while housing affordability is still a major issue, even though ​house prices have broadly stabilised. Indigenous Māori voters are also concerned about the current government’s attempts to roll back historic policies meant to improve conditions for the community as well as efforts to reduce ​the influence of the country’s founding document, the Treaty of Waitangi, on policy.

articles.title: Top Gulf official offers glimmer of hope on Trump-Iran nuclear talks as threat of war hangs over region
articles.summary: A senior United Arab Emirates official says he is cautiously optimistic about U.S.-Iran nuclear talks through Qatari mediation but won't rule out war.
articles.body: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — A senior United Arab Emirates official says he is cautiously optimistic about negotiations between the United States and Iran, citing progress through Qatari mediation over the past days, even as fears of renewed military confrontation continue to grip the Middle East. "We see some progress. … We hope that both sides will be able to reach a point where they will start building trust and engaging in a way to avoid the war, to find a political solution. … I am a little bit optimistic, but I don't exclude the other option," Dr. Ali Rashid Al Nuaimi, chairman of the Defense, Interior and Foreign Affairs Committee of the UAE's Federal National Council, told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. His remarks came as Reuters reported on Nov. 5 that Iran had submitted a new nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatar. Tehran, however, continued to insist that the U.S. meet seven conditions before negotiations could proceed, including sanctions relief and an end to the American naval blockade. IS THIS TRUMP’S LAST ‘LAST CHANCE’? CEASELESS STRING OF BROKEN CEASEFIRES FUELS DOUBT OVER IRAN DEAL President Donald Trump has not ruled out further military operations, while Iran has threatened broader retaliation if fighting resumes. For the UAE, which endured thousands of Iranian missile and drone attacks earlier this year, the possibility of a diplomatic breakthrough offers hope. But its leaders are making clear that hope cannot replace preparedness. "We plan for the worst. We hope for the best. … We always make sure that we are ready to deal with all the challenges or the threats," Al Nuaimi said. That combination of optimism and caution was evident during Fox News Digital's reporting trip across the Emirates, where daily life appeared remarkably normal despite the uncertainty surrounding the country. On an evening in downtown Dubai, restaurant terraces were packed, tourists filled the streets and crowds gathered around a fountain show set to music that moved between Arabic songs and Western pop hits. Businesses were operating, international visitors were arriving and the city continued to project an image of prosperity and openness. IRAN’S STRAIT OF HORMUZ SCHEME COULD DERAIL ONE GULF NATION’S BRIGHT FUTURE The contrast was just as striking in Abu Dhabi, where Fox News Digital attended the opening of ADIPEC 2026, one of the world's largest energy conferences, against the backdrop of continuing tensions with Iran and the disruption of the Strait of Hormuz. Days before the conference, ExxonMobil and Chevron executives had canceled their planned appearances because of security concerns, Reuters reported on Oct. 29. Yet inside the exhibition halls, delegates from around the world gathered to discuss investment, announce partnerships and explore technological solutions to the energy crisis. It was a demonstration of the UAE's determination to keep its economy moving while preparing for a security environment that has changed dramatically. TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION Preparing for another confrontation The UAE has already paid a significant price for its proximity to the conflict. More than 3,000 Iranian missiles and drones targeted the Emirates during the war, according to figures cited by The Associated Press on Nov. 2. The attacks caused casualties and damage to civilian infrastructure.Although no new Iranian attacks had targeted the UAE since May, the threat of renewed confrontation has kept the country on alert. Al Nuaimi emphasized that while the UAE considers itself a nation committed to peace, it will not hesitate to protect its population. "Every nation, when it is attacked, [has] the right to defend their people, their sovereignty, their nation," he said. But he also drew a clear distinction between the Iranian regime and the Iranian people, who are repressed by the regime. "The Iranian people deserve to be respected, accepted. They have great values, great civilization, and they are our neighbor." MIDDLE EAST TAKES CENTER STAGE AT UN AS REGIONAL LEADERS CONFRONT IRAN WAR, GAZA AND HOUTHI THREAT A partnership beyond any administration Despite the confrontation with Iran, Al Nuaimi rejected the suggestion that the UAE's relationship with Washington should be judged primarily through the current conflict or any particular U.S. administration. "We don't see our relationship with the United States through these conflicts, through security and defense. No, it's a partnership. It's a strategic partnership. It is a sustainable partnership. … Our main partnership is with the United States as a nation, with the American people." He emphasized that the relationship extends across education, medicine, technology, energy and investment, and is intended to endure political changes in Washington. "We don't look at the United States through a certain administration. Our engagement and partnership with the United States ... [is] with the nation. It's with the people. ... We have the flexibility and the ability to [adapt] and engage with any administration." The comments come at a sensitive time for Gulf governments, whose security relationships with Washington have become more consequential as Iran threatens regional infrastructure and international shipping. At ADIPEC's opening ceremony on Nov. 2, Dr. Sultan Al Jaber, the UAE's minister of industry and advanced technology and chief executive of state-owned energy giant ADNOC, emphasized that the country's ability to withstand the crisis was the result of years of preparation. "We did not write our resilience playbook during this disruption. We wrote it years before," Al Jaber told the audience. The message was consistent with what officials and analysts repeatedly emphasized during Fox News Digital's visit: the UAE intends to remain a reliable international partner despite the possibility of another regional escalation. GULF COUNTRIES STRONGLY CONDEMN IRAN'S DRONE ATTACK ON BAHRAIN AS RISING TENSIONS THREATEN MOU Security beyond military defense In a separate exclusive interview with Fox News Digital in Dubai, Mohammed Baharoon, director general of the Emirati research center B'huth, argued that the confrontation with Iran has fundamentally expanded the meaning of national security. "Our resilience now becomes our deterrence," Baharoon said. The UAE's security strategy, he explained, involves far more than intercepting missiles and drones. It also means ensuring reliable energy supplies, food security, functioning infrastructure and the ability to maintain international commerce during a crisis. For Baharoon, the conflict cannot be understood as a single confrontation between Washington and Tehran. He described three interconnected wars: the initial American-Israeli campaign against Iran, Tehran's subsequent attacks on Gulf states and Iran's disruption of international shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. "The second war was Iran's attack on the GCC, because that attack was also unprovoked," Baharoon said, referring to the Gulf Cooperation Council. He described the disruption of shipping as a separate confrontation with the global economy, arguing that the consequences extend to countries far removed from the Middle East. Despite his criticism of Tehran, Baharoon rejected the idea that Iran should permanently be treated as an enemy. Its population, economic potential and geographical importance, he argued, could make it an important contributor to regional prosperity if its leadership shifted away from confrontation. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP For the UAE, the challenge now is to prepare for the possibility of another confrontation without abandoning the diplomatic and economic relationships it has spent decades building. The crowded streets of Dubai and busy exhibition halls of Abu Dhabi reflect a country determined to move forward, even as the threat of war remains close. Whether the latest negotiations with Iran lead to a breakthrough or another round of fighting, the Emirates is betting that its resilience will allow it to weather the next crisis without losing sight of the future it is trying to build.

articles.title: Palestinian citizens of Israel put to ‘loyalty test’ after election wins
articles.summary: Palestinian citizens of Israel say Arab parties’ success in recent elections has led to growing pressure.
articles.body:
Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Israel – On election day, Lama Yassin, 31, drove to polling stations in her hometown of Arrabeh, where Palestinian citizens of Israel make up an overwhelming majority, inspired by what she was witnessing.

“You would see families coming to the polls together, grandparents and grandchildren,” she said. “It was the first time in a really long time that I felt there is hope – hope of a change.”

The overwhelming Arab turnout in the October 27 Israeli election won the Arab parties a record 19 seats in the Knesset, the Israeli parliament.

Thabet Abu Rass, an expert on Jewish-Arab relations in Israel, had predicted the Arab parties would be impossible for Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition bloc to ignore: Their seats push it past the 61-seat threshold for a ruling coalition.

Instead, Yassin and others saw Israeli channels invite “Jews to talk about Arabs and Arab voter turnout”, she recalled, with almost no Arab guests.

“The whole conversation was about how dangerous these Arab voters are.” The “most disgusting term” she saw online, however, was the repeated refrain of “election terrorism” on Channel 14, the hard-right, pro-Netanyahu station.

Within a day of the vote, Likud and figures like Itamar Ben-Gvir accused the Arab parties of stealing the election through “bribery, threats, violence, forgeries”. The accusations have continued even after the Central Elections Committee and the Israeli police said they found no sign of organised tampering.

Distraught, Yassin posted an Instagram video that went viral among Palestinians, capturing the doublespeak of Israelis they so often hear:

“Eating hummus with us? ‘Brothers and friends’.

Seeking political power? ‘Terror supporters’.

Helping someone in distress? ‘Brothers and friends’.

Voting in large numbers? ‘Terror at the ballot box’.”

“When it suits you, we are brothers and friends. When it suits you, we are a symbol of coexistence. When it suits you, you go around the world boasting about our integration into Israeli society.

“But the moment we demand to have influence, to shape policy, and to take part in decision-making – suddenly, our very presence becomes a threat.”

When voting becomes ‘a danger to the state’

More than a week after the election, Jaffa’s Ajami neighbourhood offers both the history leading up to – and the fraught circumstances of – this moment that Abu Rass calls Israel’s “political crossroads”.

Faded Arabic signs on abandoned buildings hint at the Palestinian community that thrived in Ajami before 1948. On Ajami’s streets, posters of children killed during Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza hang metres away from campaign posters for Ra’am and the Joint List.

From the back office of his cluttered hardware shop, Omar Siksik, once a Tel Aviv-Jaffa city councilman who now co-chairs Kulna Yaffa, a grassroots, Arab-Jewish civic initiative in the city, weighs this moment of unprecedented representation – met by renewed delegitimisation efforts – against Ajami’s own history. It is a struggle, he says, for basic existence.

Before 1948, Jaffa had about 100,000 Palestinians. After the Nakba, fewer than 4,000 remained – with those left fenced inside Ajami under military rule. “We called it the Ajami ghetto,” explained Siksik. Born there in 1957, he grew up sharing a toilet and kitchen with newly arrived Jewish immigrants who took the homes of expelled Palestinian neighbours.

Over time, the fence surrounding Ajami was torn down, martial law ended, and the Palestinians who remained there were granted Israeli citizenship. But later, when Siksik became the head of the Rabita Association, a nonprofit for the Palestinian residents of Jaffa, he remembered “sleeping under the bulldozers” that were razing the houses of Palestinians in the area, a practice that Rabita had fought in court.

For Siksik and others, election day is the only occasion that’s different for Palestinian citizens of Israel. “This is a democratic election,” he said. “It’s the only thing where we’re equal with the Jews. The only thing.

“When we came and expressed our dissatisfaction with this government, the Arab vote became a danger to the state,” said Siksik. “It’s not normal.”

Many Palestinian citizens of Israel believe they’ve been allowed to remain out of necessity, not equality. “The bus drivers are Arabs, the doctors in the hospitals are Arabs, the construction workers are Arabs,” Siksik notes.

But even those “essential worker” roles are being stripped away. After October 7, Israel revoked tens of thousands of work permits for Palestinians from Gaza and the West Bank to enter Israel, and the essential jobs they filled are being replaced by short-term labourers brought from abroad. Yassin notes fabricated stories over the summer on Israeli social media that Arab doctors were poisoning Jewish patients at Rambam Hospital in Haifa.

“If they could give up on anything Arab, they would,” says Yassin. “It’s not because they like us [that they let us remain]… It’s not because they want to; it’s because they have to.”

Yassin herself went through that struggle for acceptance in Israeli society. After growing up in Arrabeh, she learned Hebrew so well at Ben-Gurion University that “no one knew I was an Arab any more.” She took a job at a regional council near Jerusalem, in an entirely Jewish workplace, to prove she was “fully Israeli”.

“I did not speak Arabic in public. I even voted for [left-wing Zionist party] Meretz and favoured them over Arab parties,” said Yassin. “I wanted to be ‘the good Israeli’.”

But she could never escape that sense of otherness. At the council, colleagues asked if they could call Yassin – whose first name, Lama, means “why” in Hebrew – “Yasmine” instead, because she reminded them of Jasmine from the movie Aladdin. She was Yasmine for a year and a half. “It was another demand of giving up on another part of my identity – one that defines me literally.”

And then, the Sunday after the October 7 attacks, her colleagues would not say hello back to her.

She came to realise that “shared society cannot be built over inequality.”

After becoming director of public policy at the Abraham Initiatives, which advances the rights of Palestinian citizens in Israel, Yassin testified at Knesset committee meetings regarding unchecked crime and violence affecting their communities. She describes being dismissed or silenced outright, despite prior approval to speak. “If you say one more word,” she recalled the National Security committee chairman saying, “I will ask you to leave.”

Yassin sees that derision of a Palestinian political voice carrying over into the rhetoric – and investigations – surrounding the post-election talks. In Jaffa, that wider climate was felt on November 3, when, about midnight, about 15 security officers, a few of them masked, raided the Jaffa home of Abed Abou Shehadeh, a journalist and activist, arresting him in front of his two children. Accused of having “contacts with a foreign agent”, a court has ordered him held until November 8.

In the south, meanwhile, police arrested seven Bedouin men on suspicion of planning to pay people to vote for Ra’am, which calls them party activists and denies the allegations. Arab political leader Ayman Odeh now faces investigations as well by the Shin Bet intelligence service, which is run by the Netanyahu-aligned David Zini, over allegations that he received money from foreign sources to influence voter turnout. Odeh denies the allegations, calling them “political persecution”.

“We are now facing the whole Israeli system,” says Abu Rass. “I think we are facing the deep state also.”

Before the election, Abu Rass had predicted to Al Jazeera that 15 to 17 seats would have Israeli party leaders knocking on the Arab parties’ doors. But despite the Arab parties exceeding even those high expectations, that success has not yet borne such fruit.

With 67 members of the Knesset, including those from the Arab parties, recommending Eisenkot to the president to form a government, the anti-Netanyahu bloc has signalled agreement to remove Knesset speaker Amir Ohana and halt the judicial overhaul legislation. The Arab parties also plan to back a state inquiry into the October 7 security failures. But Abu Rass does not mistake this for a lasting partnership.

“[Eisenkot is] counting on us only for the coming months,” he says, “to help him stabilise his government, to pass this stage of removing the government and Netanyahu.”

And while Eisenkot campaigned on two pillars – removing Netanyahu, and mandating military service for ultra-Orthodox Haredim who largely do not serve – even Avigdor Liberman, long a fierce opponent of Haredi draft-dodging, now signals he would work with the Haredi parties to form an anti-Netanyahu government without the Arabs, who have repeatedly offered to support Eisenkot from outside the coalition to unseat Netanyahu.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog, tasked with choosing a leader to try to form a government, this week condemned “the coarseness and racist expressions that we have heard recently”. But according to Israeli media, during meetings with party leaders, he asked Ra’am leader Mansour Abbas whether he considers Hamas a terrorist organisation. “You cannot constantly put us to this test,” said Abbas, who has repeatedly condemned the October 7 attacks, according to Israeli media.

Yassin has felt and seen these loyalty tests play out before in Israel. “Even if the two million Arabs who live here … say ‘we condemn Hamas,’ the day after, we will have another loyalty test,” she says. “It’s never-ending, and whoever wants to deny our rights in this country does not really need a reason to.”

A Jewish-only coalition, she says, would mean “we went a few stairs down in the whole democracy approach, the so-called democracy in Israel.”

‘We don’t have the privilege of giving up’

Most people in working-class Ajami have swiftly come down from their election-night highs. “I am not optimistic,” said Nadia, a middle-aged woman sitting behind the counter of a clothing store. “If we raise our voice in the streets, we are arrested. If we raise our voice in the ballot, we are dismissed.”

Siksik fears: “I see catastrophic things coming here.”

But Nadia noted she would vote again if it means keeping Ben-Gvir and Smotrich out of government.

As Yassin puts it: “We don’t have the privilege of giving up. If we don’t do this work, no one will.”

After the sense of power the 19 seats gave people, she says, “it’s going to be hard to give it away.”

Sitting in a liberal Tel Aviv cafe, Yassin overheard a conversation at the adjacent table turn to Gaza and “how they killed the children” – apparently in reaction to what she had been saying.

As the opposition bloc appears to be pursuing every avenue to avoid including Arab parties in any position of power, she finds herself looking at even “liberal” Israelis differently.

“I was looking at every one of them and wondering if they would support an Arab or Arab parties being part of the coalition,” she said.

“Because if they don’t want my representatives, it also means that they don’t want me.”

articles.title: A couple's generosity helps build new wildlife hospital in Thailand, giving growing numbers of injured and rescued animals access to life-saving care
articles.summary: Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand (WFFT) has opened a new wildlife hospital for injured, exploited and vulnerable wildlife.
articles.body: Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand (WFFT) has opened a new wildlife hospital for injured, exploited and vulnerable wildlife. The official opening took place a few days earlier, with sponsors Monique and Arend among the guests. In March 2025, WFFT said that Monique and Arend Arling's support was funding the construction. According to the Wildlife Friends Foundation Thailand, the hospital is now treating more animals than ever before, offering urgent medical care and rehabilitation. When it announced the project, WFFT had said the number of rescued animals in its care was growing, and new species were arriving.How did a couple help fund the new wildlife hospital in ThailandA new wildlife hospital was being built at the foundation. The post was filed under the Medical category on the organisation's website, and WFFT said it was thrilled to announce the project. The foundation explained that the number of rescued animals in its care was growing and that new species were arriving. It stated that "a larger, better-equipped facility" would help it meet the increasing demands of wildlife rescue and rehabilitation.The same post named the donors behind the construction. WFFT said the project had been made possible by the generosity of Monique and Arend Arling, whose support was funding the construction of the hospital. The foundation said their contribution was laying the foundation for the facility. It added that it was deeply grateful to them for their commitment to conservation and animal welfare.What additional funding did WFFT need to equip its new wildlife hospitalThe March post said that building work was only one part of the project. According to WFFT, while construction was underway, the foundation still needed funding for essential medical equipment and interior facilities. The post stated that this funding was needed to fully equip the hospital.WFFT invited anyone who wished to be part of the project to get in touch. It said every contribution, big or small, makes a lasting impact on the lives of rescued animals, and that with this support the hospital could become a reality. Elsewhere on its website, WFFT says people can use PayPal or a credit card to make a one-off or monthly donation. The site also lists a bank transfer option for donors.How did WFFT celebrate the opening of its new wildlife hospital in ThailandWFFT said the foundation had hosted the official opening of the new WFFT Wildlife Hospital a few days earlier. The organisation described the event as "a landmark moment in our mission" to help injured, exploited and vulnerable wildlife in Thailand. Like the March announcement, the post was filed under the Medical category.According to the post, WFFT welcomed two of the main sponsors of the hospital, Monique and Arend. Many friends and supporters also attended, and the foundation said they had helped turn the dream into reality. A summary of the opening post, shown on the March page, says the time had arrived to officially open the hospital. It describes the opening as a milestone that WFFT could never have achieved without its generous donors.New WFFT wildlife hospital helping more rescued animals in ThailandWFFT said that, thanks to the kindness of Monique and Arend and the generosity of many others, the hospital is now treating more animals than ever before. The foundation described the facility as life-saving. It said every donation, large or small, had played a vital role in building a place where wildlife can receive urgent medical care, rehabilitation and a second chance at a better life. WFFT added that it was deeply grateful to everyone who had supported the project.One says Oscar, a Malayan sun bear, became the very first patient at the brand new wildlife hospital. Another asks what happens when wild animals lose their homes to human activity and looks at real-life conflicts between people and wildlife. articles.title: Pakistani astronaut to join China’s next space station mission
articles.summary: The unnamed individual will be the first foreign national to visit China’s space station as part of Shenzhou-24 mission.
articles.body:
China’s Manned Space Agency has selected a Pakistani astronaut as a payload specialist for its upcoming Shenzhou-24 mission, making the unnamed individual the first foreign national to visit the country’s space station.

The Pakistani astronaut would join China’s Shenzhou-24 mission, as part of bilateral cooperation under Beijing’s Belt and Road Initiative, Chinese state media reported on Saturday.

China has not identified the astronaut nor given a date of departure, but the mission is expected to take place by the end of the year.

Pakistani pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khurram Daud spent months training at the China Astronaut Research and Training Center in Beijing for a mission.

Last February, Pakistan and China, longstanding strategic and diplomatic partners, entered into an agreement, establishing a Chinese government-led programme to train Pakistani astronauts. China is Pakistan’s largest trading partner and a key foreign investor.

The China National Space Administration will also deploy Jinnah-1, Pakistan’s inaugural lunar rover. Weighing 35kg (77lb) and fitted with specialised scientific equipment, the rover is tasked with analysing plasma behaviour, radiation, and the composition of lunar soil.

The training programme includes practical operational exercises and intensive Chinese language lessons to prepare the candidates for the mission.

Beijing’s China Central Television reported that after completing a short-term in-orbit flight, the astronauts would return to Earth on board the Shenzhou-23 spacecraft.

China invested heavily in its space programme in recent years – catching up with its main rival, the United States – and aims to land astronauts on the Moon by 2030.

The US, Russia, and China are also racing to build nuclear reactors on the Moon. While the US space agency, NASA, announced plans to develop a nuclear reactor on the Moon by the end of 2030, Russia has been working with China and aims to do the same by 2036.

The reactors will be needed to power the mining of frozen water trapped deep in the moon’s craters, which scientists believe could supply drinking water, air, and rocket fuel for future bases. The reactors would also provide power for lunar bases.

articles.title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
articles.summary: The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden on Friday.
articles.body:
TV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air.

The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday.

"From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people.

During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show.

He added he will feature in two winter specials, expected to air between now and Christmas.

One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow , which is also the garden of his private home, which he and his wife Sarah bought in 1991.

Don replaced Alan Titchmarsh on the show in 2003, at his predecessor's request.

"I first began presenting Gardeners' World 23 years ago at Berryfields, and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago - in that time, things have changed," he recalled, on Friday's farewell.

"The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people.

"So, thank you. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time... goodbye."

Details of the next series of Gardeners' World will be announced at a later date, the BBC noted in a statement ahead of Don's farewell. His successor has not yet been named.

Bookmakers and viewers have pointed to regular co-presenters like Frances Tophill and Adam Frost as top contenders, though Tophill has played down expectations of stepping directly into his shoes.

Prior to fronting Gardeners' World, Don hosted other shows including Tomorrow's World, Holiday and - a preview of coming attractions - a gardening segment on This Morning.

He took a three-year break from the programme after suffering a minor stroke in 2008.

In September this year, Don announced that the current series would be his last. In a statement, he said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience", but added that "now is the right time for a change".

The BBC said at the time that Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003.

Don was made an OBE by Queen Elizabeth, in 2018, for services to horticulture, broadcasting and charity. And he also received the RHS Victoria Medal of Honour - highest honour in horticulture.

His final episode of Gardeners' World is available to stream now on BBC iPlayer.
