articles.title: AI, electricity bills and voter anger: How data centres tanked Trump's midterm hopes
articles.summary: America's artificial intelligence revolution was supposed to make the United States more powerful, strengthen its economy and help it stay ahead of China.
articles.body: America's artificial intelligence revolution was supposed to make the United States more powerful, strengthen its economy and help it stay ahead of China. Instead, the massive infrastructure powering that revolution has emerged as an unexpected political liability for Donald Trump, with angry voters turning against data centres and handing Democrats a powerful weapon in the 2026 midterm elections.According to a report by CNN, Democrats successfully turned public opposition to data centre construction into an election issue, targeting Republican candidates who supported the industry's expansion.In Texas, James Talarico's campaign used the growing resentment against data centres to take on Republican Ken Paxton, while similar anti-data centre campaigns gained ground in other states.The campaign was part of a broader Democratic strategy that connected the expansion of AI infrastructure to rising household costs, electricity bills and concerns about corporate influence. The issue gained traction beyond Texas, with Democrats using opposition to data centres in competitive races across Ohio, Michigan, South Carolina and other states.Why are Americans increasingly turning against data centres?The rapid expansion of data centres has triggered growing opposition among American communities, with residents questioning whether the economic benefits of the AI boom are worth the costs they could face. What technology companies see as essential infrastructure for the future, many local residents increasingly view as a threat to their electricity bills, water supplies and neighbourhoods.One of the biggest concerns is electricity consumption. Data centres require enormous amounts of power to operate thousands of servers and cooling systems around the clock.As more facilities come up, demand for electricity rises, putting additional pressure on local power grids. Residents fear that utilities will have to invest in expensive infrastructure to meet this demand, with some of the costs potentially passed on to ordinary households through higher electricity bills.Water consumption has emerged as another major concern. Many data centres use water-based cooling systems to prevent servers from overheating. In regions already struggling with water shortages, residents worry that large facilities could put further pressure on limited supplies.The backlash also extends to environmental and neighbourhood concerns. Residents have raised questions about noise from cooling equipment, backup generators, construction activity and the conversion of large stretches of land into industrial facilities.They have also questioned the tax incentives offered to technology companies, arguing that these projects may generate enormous profits for corporations without creating enough permanent jobs or economic benefits for local communities.Why is the US building so many data centres?The United States is rapidly expanding its data centre infrastructure because of the growing demand for artificial intelligence, cloud computing and digital services.The AI boom has significantly increased the need for computing power, with companies requiring thousands of specialised computer chips and powerful servers to train AI models, process information and generate responses.The expansion is also driven by America's competition with China. The Trump administration views AI as a strategic technology that could shape future economic growth, military capabilities and global influence. Building more data centres is therefore seen as essential to maintaining US leadership in the global AI race.Technology giants such as Microsoft, Google, Amazon and Meta are pouring billions of dollars into new facilities to support their AI ambitions. articles.title: How Yoshitomo Nara’s ‘big-headed girls’ took over the world
articles.summary: The iconic characters are conquering new territory at the artist’s first major solo show in New York City in close to a decade.
articles.body: The big-headed, wide-eyed girls that made Yoshitomo Nara one of the most beloved Japanese artists of the 21st century are everywhere — if you know where to look. You can find them on T-shirts, skateboards, plastered on water bottles as stickers, or blown up and rendered in monumental scale in the artist’s sculptural works. You can even find them, scrawled by the artist himself in confident, graphic lines, on the walls of a Manhattan dive bar he visited in 2009. (On his way back from the impromptu bar decorating, he was arrested for graffitiing on the subway walls and barely made it out in time to his next gallery opening). Angry, spiteful, mischievous, bored, confused: Nara’s figures are both enigmatic and instantly legible, recognizable both for the artist’s distinct style and their punching emotional effect. Now, Nara’s characters are conquering new territory with a retrospective at David Zwirner Gallery, his first major solo show in New York City in close to a decade. The exhibition, which dovetails with a show at the Hirshhorn Museum and Sculpture Garden in Washington, DC, features new, unseen works along with older pieces. There are both tiny drawings on torn fragments of paper as well as huge, richly painted portraits whose luminescent eyes seem to follow you around the room. At the Zwirner show’s opening night Thursday, Nara fans queued for close to an hour in a line that extended two blocks, some holding umbrellas to ward off the rain. It was a distinctly young and stylish crowd: There was no shortage of Labubus dangling from bags (the characters’ own huge eyes slightly Nara-esque) and tabi ballet flats. A few subway stops away at Niagara — the East Village bar that Nara graffitied a decade ago — a steady stream of devotees made pilgrimages before or after the opening, a bartender said. There they found a series of graphic drawings, now protected behind plastic, of Nara figures rocking out. These isolated, defiant figures have become a throughline for the artist’s nearly four-decade career. They are, in Nara’s telling, self-portraits of a sort, ciphers for his own emotions in the aftermath of Japan’s wartime history and multiple environmental disasters. For the waves of young fans who flock to Nara exhibits and emblazon his images on their belongings, they’re a representation of something different: The ennui and turmoil that has defined Gen Z’s coming-of-age in a turbulent world marked by existential threats at every turn. No matter how they’re perceived, the artworks have made Nara a significant name in the art world, with his work selling for millions, such as “Knife Behind Back,” a huge painting of a frowning girl, one arm tucked behind her back, which went for a whopping $24.94m at an auction in 2019 (a record high for the artist). It’s classic Nara, featuring a figure who is both adorable and slightly menacing, resisting the reduction of herself to something simple and endearing. The camouflage of cuteness On the surface, the images with “the big eyes, the round faces,” can be written off as merely cute, according to Mika Yoshitake, an independent curator specializing in postwar and contemporary Japanese art, and curator of the artist’s 2021 LACMA retrospective and forthcoming 2027 exhibition at SFMOMA . But they “actually refuse the genre” that historically flattens representations of women and girls. You can see that subversion, Yoshitake said, in his characters’ signature haunting eyes, rendered with the subtlety of a master painter. They sometimes have “sidelong glares, very deadpan, sometimes aggressive,” she said. “The cuteness is more like a camouflage for something that’s more guarded.” Nara grew up the 1960s and 70s in rural northern Japan, during the delicate decades after World War II. The war haunts his work, said Yoshitake: “There’s lots of hidden messages about solitude and bearing the history of the loss that Japan had felt.” Nara’s experiences in Germany, where he studied at the prestigious Kunstakademie Düsseldorf in the late 80s, further added to the political dimensions of his work (“Stop the Bombs,” an acrylic painting from 2019 later repurposed as a design for one of his collaborations with fashion designer Stella McCartney, is one example of the more literal political messaging of his art, what Yoshitake calls his “resistance to the system, or to war, or to things that he feels wrong in society”). His images of lonely children, sometimes bearing surreptitious knives or axes, are “about being tired of injustice, being resilient towards it, and saying, okay, you know what, life isn’t fair, but we will fight back,” said Kevin Lenaerts, the creative director at the Skateroom, which creates highly coveted limited-edition skateboards in collaboration with artists. Their Nara collab was one of their most successful, he said. Nara’s work has an innate resonance with counterculture, modulated by the rock music that was a lifeline for him as a young boy in rural Japan. He’s “a real punk,” said Lenaerts. World politics and events have continued to influence Nara’s work. The monumental sculptures on view in DC — the largest is, at 13 feet, as tall as an elephant — were created as a response to the 2011 Fukushima nuclear disaster in Japan. After the catastrophe, which displaced tens of thousands of people, Nara “began playing with clay as a way of being able to reconnect to very simple therapeutic gestures,” said Aaron Seeto, the Hirshhorn’s acting director. Nara’s work also has an accessibility that extends outside the immediate political context in which it incubated. You don’t have to understand postwar Japan to be instantly drawn in by his beguiling figures, or to feel your own troubled emotions reflected in them. Nara’s new generation Nara’s poster-punk aesthetic made his works popular with previous generations of rebels, landing on the album covers of bands like Shonen Knife and R.E.M. His works have also found a new wave of fervent fans among Gen Z. Yoshitake, the curator, attributes the artist’s appeal among younger generations in part to his works’ “graphic legibility.” At the same time, the emotions of his art “speaks to this generation that is fluent in vulnerability,” she said. And, in a hypercapitalistic world where everything’s a product, his figures retain an authenticity. There’s “this resistance to a type of slickness that some of these more popular branded images have,” said Yoshitake. “It’s never trend-driven, and that’s why it’s timeless,” she added. Nara, for all the explication of his figures as self-portraits, also seems to have a particular aptitude for capturing the contradictions of girlhood. Amanda Quach, a Los Angeles-based fashion and lifestyle content creator whose videos include a roll call of all her Nara merch, said she first discovered Nara’s work at LACMA’s 2021-2022 retrospective. In the aftermath of the Covid-19 pandemic , she felt isolated and disaffected. In Nara’s paintings and drawings, she saw younger versions of herself. He has a startling ability, she said, to “capture what it feels like to be a young girl with those complex, frustrating emotions, but looking so cute and innocent at the same time.” Quach is such a Nara fan that she has two of his works tattooed on her: The smoking girl from “Too Young to Die” on her arm, and a girl rocking out on stage on her leg. She’s not the only one. Camila Duarte, a New York City-based tattoo artist, said she’s inked over a dozen Nara figures, most of them also on young women. His work reminds her of the feeling of being a child, and particularly of feeling like a child thrust into a dangerous, mystifying world. “There’s so much going on in the world,” she added. “We’re all maybe just feeling a little rebellious too.”

articles.title: When will winter weather arrive? November forecast has unusual answer
articles.summary: Widespread chilly weather still seems a long way away despite what the calendar says. One of the warmest Novembers on record is expected in the U.S.
articles.body:
Widespread chilly weather still seems a long way away despite what the calendar says, as the nation is forecast to see one of the warmest Novembers on record, thanks mainly to the warming impacts of El Niño , forecasters said.

"The ongoing El Niño remains the dominant teleconnection to influence this forecast (for November)," said Johnna Infanti, a forecaster from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's Climate Prediction Center , in an online report .

Chad Merrill, a senior meteorologist from AccuWeather , told USA TODAY that "a very warm month is expected nationally. It will likely rank in the top 10 for warmest Novembers."

Where are above-average temperatures expected in November?

The temperature forecast map from the Climate Prediction Center (above) shows orange for nearly the entire nation, meaning above-average temperatures are likely practically coast-to-coast.

On the map, only the Southwest is not forecast to see above-normal temperatures. In the Southwest, there are "equal chances" of seeing warmer-than-average or cooler-than-average temperatures.

No part of the U.S. is forecast to see below-average temperatures this month.

Specifically, Merrill told USA TODAY that "Northern California into the Northwest into the northern portion of the Plains through the Mississippi Valley and into the East will be warmer than the historical average for temperatures."

Which areas are forecast to see above-average precipitation in November?

According to the Climate Prediction Center map, the wettest parts of the nation in November will be the Southwest and the central and northern Plains.

The only states that should see a drier-than-average November are Michigan and Montana, the CPC map shows.

AccuWeather also said that Southern California coastal flooding remains a concern: Coastal flooding is expected to continue into November, with some of the highest coastal water levels of the season forecast to occur around Nov. 25, AccuWeather said.

From parched lands to raging seas, photos show El Niño’s grip on 2026

Are there any major storms in the forecast?

"Our long-range team expects at least one sizable storm to bring copious snow to the Mountain West and heavy rain that will trigger some flooding to the West, particularly California, the Great Basin and Southwest," Merrill said.

In the East, Merrill said there will likely be a storm closer to Thanksgiving week that brings heavy rain to the Southeast and Mid-Atlantic states.

Thanksgiving weekend could bring a taste of winter, AccuWeather said. Colder air could bring flurries or snow to parts of the Great Lakes and Northeast.

What's causing this mild pattern across much of the nation?

"A highly energized Pacific jet stream triggered by both the strong El Niño and marine heat waves in the Pacific are flooding much of the U.S. with warmer-than-average temperatures in November," Merrill told USA TODAY.

Looking ahead to December and beyond, the warmth is expected to continue, as El Niño tends to make winters warmer in the U.S., especially across the northern half of the nation. This is due to unusually warm water temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean, which shifts the jet stream and makes extended invasions of cold, Arctic air less likely to occur.

Doyle Rice is a national correspondent for USA TODAY, with a focus on weather and climate.

articles.title: Rains flood 70,000 displaced families’ tents in Gaza
articles.summary: Initial losses are estimated at about $3m, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.
articles.body:
About 70,000 tents sheltering displaced Palestinians have been flooded in the Gaza Strip within 12 hours of the first winter storm of the season, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office.

In a statement on Saturday, the office said initial losses were estimated at about $3m. Dozens of walls had collapsed and people had been injured, it said, while cracked buildings at risk of collapse posed a growing danger.

The office held Israel “fully responsible” for what it called a disaster caused by the continued closure of crossings and the blocking of shelter and reconstruction materials. It urged the international community and UN agencies to intervene immediately to protect the displaced.

Gaza’s civil defence agency said its crews received about 1,500 distress calls in just 10 hours after the rain began early on Saturday, with water levels in several shelter sites rising by 30-40cm (12-16 inches).

“What we feared has actually happened,” civil defence spokesman Mahmoud Basal told Al Jazeera. “A few shelter centres were completely flooded, and everyone inside them has now been forced out into the unknown.”

Basal said premature babies, the elderly and the sick were most at risk. “Those living in tents are at risk of death at any moment, and of illness at any moment,” he said.

The storm also brought down buildings damaged in Israel’s genocidal war on the enclave that began in October 2023.

The civil defence agency said rescuers had evacuated residents of a building in the central Nuseirat area that partially collapsed in the strong winds and rain. In northern Gaza, the wall of a separate building fell down due to heavy rainfall, injuring two people, according to the Palestinian news agency Wafa.

Footage from camps in Gaza City, Khan Younis and Deir el-Balah showed families wading through ankle-deep water, mattresses and blankets soaked, and children standing barefoot in pools of mud and sewage.

“Even houses can’t hold up against this rain, so how can open plastic sheeting?” said Al Jazeera’s Nour Khaled, reporting from a camp in Gaza City. She said more than 28,000 widows were among those facing the winter alone with their children.

In al-Mawasi, the coastal area where more than 900,000 displaced people are sheltering in southern Gaza, rain had been falling since 10pm (20:00 GMT) on Friday, Al Jazeera’s Rami Abu Taima reported from Khan Younis.

“People woke up to find hundreds, even thousands, of tents flooded across the Gaza Strip,” he said. He added that more than 125,000 families living along the coast were at particular risk of having their tents swept away by the sea.

Gaza’s emergency committee said more than one million displaced people face a harsh winter, and that the territory urgently needs about 200,000 tents along with heating supplies.

Raed al-Dahshan, director of civil defence in Gaza, told Al Jazeera that crews could do little once they reached flooded families. “Civil defence does not have a single tarpaulin or a single tent,” he said. “We deal only with saving lives, and that is not enough.”

The storm also hit Gaza’s battered health system. Mohammed Abu Salmiya, director of al-Shifa Medical Complex in Gaza City, told Al Jazeera that the hospital’s emergency department flooded and was out of service for about four hours. He warned of a rise in gastrointestinal, respiratory and skin infections as sewage mixed with rainwater inside tents.

“We will see many deaths, in the dozens and perhaps the hundreds, among newborns who need warmth in these tents,” he said.

Reporting from Gaza City port, Al Jazeera’s Ghazi al-Aloul said thousands of families had pitched tents along the shoreline, where they face strong winds and rising tides. “These tents will flood first from the rain, and second from seawater,” he said.

Many of the tents were put up in the first year of displacement and are now in their fourth, patched and re-stitched by their owners. Under the ceasefire’s humanitarian protocol, they were supposed to be replaced with caravans, which Israel has not allowed into the territory.

One displaced man on the beach told Al Jazeera: “They pushed us west towards the sea. Why don’t they just throw us into the sea and be done with it?”

Mohammed Salha, director of the Palestinian NGO Network, told Al Jazeera that only 180 to 200 trucks were entering Gaza daily, far short of the 600 agreed under the humanitarian protocol of the “ceasefire”, and that only about 40 of those carried humanitarian aid.

“We don’t want to respond after the tents flood,” Salha said, adding that 50,000 tents had been waiting on the Egyptian side of the border. “We must respond before the disaster happens.”

He described international pressure on Israel to allow in more supplies as “timid”.

articles.title: 'Remove your Italian lenses': BJP slams Sonia Gandhi for remarks on country's progress
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Saturday hit back at Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi over her criticism of the PM Modi government, asking her
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Saturday hit back at Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi over her criticism of the PM Modi government, asking her to "remove Italian lenses" and acknowledge India's progress over the past 12 years. The party also criticised her remarks on the Emergency and questioned the contents of her upcoming memoir, 'Belonging: A Journey of Love'."If you take off your Italian lenses, you will see India clearly: Sabka Saath, Sabka Vikas, Sabka Prayas, and India rising as a global power at a 7.8 per cent (GDP) growth rate," news agency PTI quoted BJP Rajya Sabha MP Tarun Chugh as saying.Chugh accused the Congress of using caste, religion and vote-bank politics to divide the country and asked Gandhi to address alleged scams during her party's rule, the 1984 anti-Sikh riots and the Bhopal gas tragedy in her memoir.He also questioned her silence on the deaths of Indian soldiers and raised the Batla House encounter, asking why she had allegedly cried after a terrorist was killed."Gandhi is unable to digest the rise of Sanatan under the BJP-NDA rule," Chugh said.Sonia, in an interview with the news outlet The Hindu ahead of her book's launch, alleged that the last 12 years had caused "great damage" to India's democratic fabric and institutions. She said restoring the country's systems would take time even after the Modi government leaves office, adding that people were beginning to recognise the damage.The BJP also targeted the Congress leader over her remarks on the Emergency, imposed on June 25, 1975. In the interview, she said the suspension of democratic rights and habeas corpus during the period had been carried out constitutionally. articles.title: Israel's nuclear secret is now Washington's biggest headache. What changed after 60 years?
articles.summary: In 1960, a mysterious construction site in Israel's Negev desert caught the attention of American officials.
articles.body: In 1960, a mysterious construction site in Israel's Negev desert caught the attention of American officials. When questioned about the facility near Dimona, Israeli officials had a rather unusual explanation. It was a textile factory.But behind that explanation, Israel was building the foundations of a nuclear programme that would remain hidden from public scrutiny for decades. Washington knew about it, successive American administrations chose not to challenge it publicly, and Israel continued to neither confirm nor deny possessing nuclear weapons.More than six decades later, that carefully maintained silence is becoming harder to protect. The United States, which helped preserve Israel's nuclear ambiguity for generations, is now facing questions over its position as it fights alongside Israel against Iran.With American lawmakers demanding answers, questions emerging over nuclear double standards and Saudi Arabia pursuing its own nuclear ambitions, the old understanding between Washington and Tel Aviv is facing a serious test.The latest CNN investigation by Davis Winkie, traces how this decades-old arrangement is now coming under pressure from multiple directions.In a June congressional hearing, US secretary of state Marco Rubio acknowledged that Israel's nuclear capabilities are widely believed to exist, even though neither country has officially confirmed them.Responding to questions from Democratic Congressman Joaquin Castro, Rubio said, "I think most of the world assesses that they do, but we've never, they've never, acknowledged that publicly." He added that Washington does not discuss the matter as part of its foreign policy.The questions are no longer confined to whether Israel possesses nuclear weapons. They increasingly concern the implications of maintaining silence while the US is directly involved in a war alongside Israel against Iran.Castro, who serves on the House foreign affairs and intelligence committees, told CNN that the policy of nuclear ambiguity had become "reckless and dangerous".He questioned how Washington could fight alongside Israel without knowing its nuclear red lines or explaining what contingency plans were in place if those weapons were deployed or its nuclear facilities came under attack.The pressure has also moved to Capitol Hill. On May 4, more than two dozen Democratic lawmakers, led by Castro, wrote to Rubio seeking information about Israel's nuclear capabilities, its potential use of nuclear weapons and the administration's contingency planning.In their letter, the lawmakers warned that "the risks of miscalculation, escalation, and nuclear use in this environment are not theoretical". They argued that Washington could not develop a coherent non-proliferation policy for the Middle East while maintaining official silence about the nuclear capabilities of a country fighting alongside it.Why Israel chose to keep its nuclear arsenal a secretFor Israel, maintaining nuclear ambiguity was a calculated strategy to enjoy the advantages of nuclear deterrence without facing the diplomatic and regional consequences of openly declaring itself a nuclear power.By neither confirming nor denying possession of nuclear weapons, Israel could keep its adversaries uncertain about its capabilities while avoiding international pressure and a potential arms race in the Middle East.A major concern was that publicly acknowledging its nuclear arsenal could encourage Arab countries to pursue similar capabilities and draw greater Soviet involvement in the region during the Cold War.A declassified July 1969 memorandum by then US national security adviser Henry Kissinger to President Richard Nixon reflected these concerns. Kissinger argued that Washington should prevent Israel's nuclear possession from becoming an "established international fact", fearing the consequences of openly acknowledging it.Israel also wanted to avoid international scrutiny, particularly as the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) took shape in the 1960s. The treaty, which opened for signature in 1968, recognised five countries as nuclear-weapon states under its framework. Israel never signed the treaty and continued to maintain ambiguity over its arsenal. Its approach helped it avoid the diplomatic complications that an official declaration could have triggered.Washington eventually became central to preserving this arrangement. While President John F Kennedy initially pressed Israel to allow inspections of its Dimona facility, the approach changed under President Richard Nixon.During a September 1969 meeting with Prime Minister Golda Meir, the two governments reached an understanding that Israel would not publicly declare, test or advertise its nuclear weapons, while Washington would avoid publicly challenging its nuclear status.More than six decades later, Israel continues to follow this policy, with the UK House of Commons Library estimating its arsenal at around 90 warheads.You use AI every day. articles.title: From a laundry worker's daughter to a banking pioneer: How Maggie Lena Walker established a bank in segregated America in 1903
articles.summary: Maggie Lena Walker rose from modest beginnings in Richmond, Virginia, to become one of America's most influential African American business leaders.
articles.body: Maggie Lena Walker rose from modest beginnings in Richmond, Virginia, to become one of America's most influential African American business leaders. Born in 1864, shortly after the American Civil War, she grew up in a society shaped by racial discrimination and limited opportunities for Black women. In 1903, she established the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank, becoming the first African American woman in the United States to charter a bank. Her achievement helped transform financial opportunities for Black families and demonstrated how collective savings could support economic independence.How Maggie Lena Walker established a bank in segregated AmericaWalker grew up in Richmond, where her mother, Elizabeth Draper Mitchell, worked as a laundress after gaining freedom from slavery. The National Park Service records that Walker's early experiences exposed her to the difficulties faced by working families and influenced her understanding of financial security.She attended Richmond's public schools for African Americans and trained as a teacher. After graduating, she taught for several years before leaving the profession following her marriage to Armstead Walker in 1886.Her ambitions extended beyond education. Walker joined the Independent Order of St. Luke, a mutual aid organisation that provided assistance, insurance and burial support to African Americans. According to Encyclopedia Virginia, she became its Right Worthy Grand Secretary in 1899, taking responsibility for an organisation that needed stronger financial management.A mutual aid organisation became the foundation for her ambitionsWalker worked to improve the Independent Order of St. Luke's finances and expanded its membership. She strengthened the organisation and encouraged greater participation, particularly among women.She believed economic progress required more than individual effort. In 1901, she outlined plans for a newspaper, a bank and a department store that could support Black businesses and create opportunities within the community.The St. Luke Herald, launched in 1902, became an important part of this vision. The newspaper communicated with members, promoted African American businesses and encouraged readers to participate in the organisation's activities. Her approach centred on encouraging ordinary people to save money rather than relying exclusively on wealthy investors.How did she prepare to run a bankWalker understood that establishing a financial institution required practical knowledge. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation records that she studied banking operations at Richmond's Merchants National Bank, learning about financial procedures and management.Her preparation was particularly significant because banking leadership was dominated by men, while African American women faced additional barriers under segregation.On 2 November 1903, the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank opened in Richmond. According to the National Park Service, nearly 300 customers attended its opening.The Richmond Federal Reserve reports that the bank received more than $8,000 in deposits on its first day. Contributions ranged from small amounts to larger sums, demonstrating how customers with different incomes could participate in the institution.Walker became its first president, making her the first African American woman in the United States to establish and lead a bank.Small deposits helped Black families build financial securityThe bank offered African American customers an opportunity to save money and access credit at a time when mainstream financial institutions frequently excluded them.The FDIC explains that St. Luke Penny Savings Bank provided loans to Black homeowners and businesses, supporting economic activity in Richmond's Jackson Ward neighbourhood.Its growth was substantial. According to the FDIC, deposits rose from more than $9,000 at its opening to $170,000 within three years. By 1920, the bank had financed more than 600 home loans to residents of Jackson Ward.The Smithsonian National Museum of American History reports that deposits eventually reached half a million dollars by the mid-1920s. The achievement reflected the financial strength that could emerge when working families pooled their savings. Walker also believed women should participate directly in business and economic leadership.How Walker protected her bank during the Great DepressionWalker remained involved in the bank's operations as it expanded, but economic difficulties eventually threatened its stability.The Smithsonian records that she recognised declining assets before the 1929 stock market crash and began considering a merger with other Black-owned financial institutions in Richmond.In 1931, St. Luke Penny Savings Bank merged with Second Street Savings Bank and Commercial Bank and Trust to form Consolidated Bank and Trust Company. Walker became chairperson of its board of directors.The Richmond Federal Reserve credits her with helping protect the institution through the merger. Consolidated Bank and Trust continued operating for decades, preserving an important part of her banking legacy.Her influence extended beyond bankingWalker also supported civil rights, education and community development. The National Park Service records her involvement with the National Association of Colored Women, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People and the Virginia Industrial School for Girls.She encouraged African American women to pursue education, business opportunities and leadership roles, while supporting organisations that worked to improve their communities.In 1928, an illness left Walker using a wheelchair, but she continued participating in public and organisational affairs. She died in Richmond on 15 December 1934, aged 70. Her former residence is now preserved as the Maggie L. Walker National Historic Site, managed by the National Park Service.Walker’s banking legacy continued after her death. The FDIC notes that Consolidated Bank and Trust remained the oldest continuously African American-operated bank in the United States until 2009.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Dozens killed as humanitarian crisis mounts in Yemen: What next for war?
articles.summary: Government forces reclaim key territories in Taiz and Lahij but face setbacks under Houthi resistance in certain areas.
articles.body:
Dozens were killed in Yemen on Friday when a missile struck a market in Taiz governorate, with each side of Yemen’s brutal war blaming the other for the attack.

It has been a month since Yemen’s internationally recognised government launched its “Dawn of Yemen” offensive on the Iran-aligned Houthi rebel group after it took swaths of territory along the country’s Red Sea coast.

As the fighting continues, the humanitarian crisis is only intensifying, with hundreds of thousands displaced so far.

Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council has said the government will continue with its “irreversible” drive to dismantle Houthi military capacity and restore sovereignty, meaning the war may get worse before there is any resolution, observers say.

The operation was launched by the head of the Presidential Leadership Council of Yemen’s internationally recognised government, Rashad al-Alimi, on October 5.

Its aim is to recapture areas under Houthi control and liberate the capital city of Sanaa, which has been under the rebels’ control since September 2014.

The operation has relied on air support from the Saudi-led coalition, as well as ground operations carried out by government military coalitions and units to weaken the Houthis’ military capabilities.

In the Red Sea corridor, breaking the Houthis’ maritime chokehold and securing the Bab al-Mandeb strait has been an essential goal after the group captured the strategic port city of Mocha (Mokha) in September.

How much territory have the government forces taken back?

After launching the operation, the government said its forces recaptured positions around Dhubab and Bab al-Mandeb the same day, though the extent of their gains could not be confirmed.

It also said they captured mountain positions in Haifan, western Taiz and around al-Waziiya.

By October 13, fighting spread to Marib, where the government forces claimed gains around the Maas camp and north of Harib.

It did, however, lose territory in Taiz governorate, which led to a Houthi siege that continues to suffocate the city as it reaches its first month.

On Friday, the government forces said they had recaptured many areas in the governorate, including al-Nidani village, Shaab al-Sarari, large parts of the Sanamat area and the Ribat al-Qarn area in Dhi al-Barh in Taiz governorate.

Government troops and coalition fighters also secured the Tavat Wathib and Habil al-Saram hills along the Al-Aqroud front.

They announced the execution of 1,211 operations against Houthi positions on the different battlefronts, as they confirmed control over new positions on the Tur al-Bahah front in the Lahij governorate.

However, government forces are far from being able to take back Yemen’s capital, Sanaa, Thomas Bonnie James, an assistant professor in politics and international relations at Aberdeen University in the United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.

“[Defeat] won’t happen if it means taking back Sanaa and ending Houthi rule. Not any time soon,” he said. “The government’s forces look big on paper, but they are spread across too many fronts and use old equipment.

“Sanaa is surrounded by mountains, which makes it easy to defend. A much stronger Saudi-Emirati coalition tried from 2015 and never came close,” he explained.

What else has the government achieved since the operation began?

James told Al Jazeera that Dawn of Yemen’s aim is to apply pressure to, rather than achieve the total defeat of, the Houthis.

“Dawn of Yemen is better understood as a way to apply pressure than as a bid for total victory,” he said. “The aim is to make the war more costly for the Houthis and to give Saudi Arabia a stronger position before any peace deal.

“What happens in the next three months matters more than the slogans.”

The Yemeni Presidential Leadership Council announced on Thursday that the armed forces have carried out 40,761 military operations since the beginning of Dawn of Yemen.

The council also said the attacks resulted in the “neutralisation” of about 20,000 Houthi leaders and elements, and more than 5,000 vehicles.

Previous announcements from the military command said they conducted 17,000 targeting operations during their first weeks and daily figures ranging between 951 and 1,272 operations throughout the month.

Last month, the Yemeni government also said its forces were able to kill or wound 1,540 Houthis in 24 hours.

Last week, the government said 16,100 Houthi operatives and commanders had been killed or wounded since October 5.

The Houthis did say that the total number of attacks the group has been subjected to since the beginning of the escalation reached 3,930 raids and missiles up until early November.

Al Jazeera has not been able to verify these figures.

The Houthis, who are also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have caused hundreds of casualties since the beginning of the escalation.

Yemen’s government forces have blamed the Houthis for an attack on the al-Hadara market on Friday in the Taiz governorate that killed and injured dozens, mostly civilians.

Government military spokesperson, Colonel Majed al-Nazili, said the “terrorist” Houthis hit the market with ballistic missiles, calling it a war crime.

The Iran-backed Houthis rejected the accusation and said Saudi Arabia, which backs the Yemeni government, was responsible for the attack.

After taking the capital and state institutions in 2014, the Houthis have had access to a large number of weapons that once belonged to the Yemeni military.

Analysts say with the external support from Iran and their reliance on international black markets, the Houthis’ military capabilities continued to advance .

Their increasingly long-range missile strikes have allowed them to reach many areas across Saudi Arabia and even Israel in June.

One of the Houthis’ latest deadly attacks killed at least 70 government security recruits in Shabwah.

As the government and the Houthis continue fighting, the humanitarian situation in Yemen is heading towards catastrophe.

More than 323,000 people have been displaced in Yemen since the escalation began in August, with Taiz governorate taking in most of them, the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported on Friday.

More than two in five of the internally displaced in Yemen are in Taiz, where the Houthi blockade continues to encircle the city, cutting off supplies to about 800,000 people.

The UN Human Rights Office has reported 281 civilian casualties since August, with 69 people killed and 212 injured. Children make up more than one-third of casualties.

In Taiz, Salah Ahmed Ghaleb al-Majidi, acting director of the governorate’s Siege Affairs Department, described the situation to Al Jazeera as “catastrophic”.

Essentials, including medical supplies, food, fuel and water, are unable to reach the governorate due to the Houthi blockade.

An Al Jazeera report found that the remaining diesel stocks in the city have dwindled and have less than 48 hours left to run.

Hospitals are warning that once they run out of fuel, departments and medical centres will have to shut down, including emergency services.

Taiz’s deputy governor for health affairs, Ilan Abdul Haw, told Al Jazeera that about 40 percent of hospitals have closed, while those still open are operating at 50 percent capacity due to the lack of fuel.

James told Al Jazeera that as the winter approaches in Yemen, and the siege on Taiz tightens, conditions will only worsen for Yemenis caught in the conflict.

“The biggest worry is the people of Taiz. More than 800,000 of them have been cut off from aid since the Houthis surrounded the city in early October,” he said. “Winter is coming, aid money is short, and the city is under siege. That is what more fighting will mean for ordinary Yemenis.”

The war has also spread beyond Yemen, as the Houthis continue strikes on Saudi airports and oil sites.

“The Houthis are firing at Saudi almost every day. Saudi Arabia is now openly bombing inside Yemen again for the first time since 2022,” James said. “Both sides are hitting where it hurts most, and that is how wars get bigger”.

Other fighting in the region could also pull Yemen into a wider war, and vice versa, as the US-Israel war on Iran remains in a deadlock, James told Al Jazeera.

“Yemen is now tied to the wider conflict with Iran. If the US strikes Iran again, Iran will want to use the Houthis to put more pressure on Saudi Arabia,” he said.

articles.title: He left NYC after 9/11 for a new life in South America
articles.summary: In our roundup of travel stories this week: the Englishman who walked around the world, why Norway is making toilets “great again,” plus a New Yorker driven to start over in Argentina in the wake of 9/11.
articles.body: In our roundup of travel stories this week: The Englishman who walked around the world, why Norway is making toilets “great again,” plus a New Yorker driven to start life over in Argentina in the wake of 9/11. Finding solace in Mendoza David English planned to sign a “career-clinching contract” on the morning of September 11, 2001. An entrepreneur, English worked in Lower Manhattan, and the move was going to change his life. Instead, he woke up to the terror attacks that changed the city and the lives of so many. English watched fighter jets flying over his New York apartment, and endured weeks of “false alarms and alerts” while breathing in the fumes drifting over from the site. So a year later, he abandoned his American life – and the “horrible climate of fear” that took over the US after 9/11 – to start anew in Argentina. And he never left, settling in Mendoza. Now he has a son – who was born in Argentina and wouldn’t have been born had it not been for the fateful decision English made in the wake of the attacks. Read about the solace he found in Mendoza and the life he built there. Around the world in 28 years In 1998, adventurer Karl Bushby set off on foot around the world. Twenty-eight years and 31,000 miles later, he completed his journey this week, arriving at his mother’s home in northern England. Watch his CNN interview here. Another ambitious traveler, German videographer David Bossek is halfway through his four-year trip around the world, which he’s trying to complete almost entirely overland and by sea, tracking his carbon footprint along the way with the goal of compensating for his environmental impact. However, not everything has gone to plan. (For subscribers only). And Georgia man Cory Lee has visited 56 countries and all seven continents and is still only 36. His achievement is all the more impressive as he accomplished it while using a 400-pound power wheelchair — navigating not just the globe but formidable accessibility barriers. He told CNN what his biggest challenges have been. Destination inspiration Prefer to explore the world just one city at a time? Then we have some recommendations for you. Busan is South Korea’s second-largest city and is a laid-back alternative to the bustle of the capital. In the words of one travel expert, “It offers something totally different — it’s by the coast, has beaches, a slower-paced way of life, and the people are much more vivacious.” In Colorado, Aspen is famous the world over for its glitz, glamour and top-tier skiing. However, its 20th-century roots as a countercultural hub are still going strong. “Freaks are people that don’t want to live in the traditional, cookie-cutter lifestyle of suburban America,” says DJ Watkins, a local author, curator and gallerist. “And Aspen has always attracted people like that.” Finally, a European pick. In the CNN series “Eva Longoria: Searching for Spain,” Longoria visited Seville, the largest city in Andalucia and home of flamenco and tapas. It’s also world-famous for its glorious mix of Moorish and Gothic architecture. CNN subscribers can watch here. Beijing’s World Park This Chinese theme park has more than 100 replicas of global landmarks which, when the park first opened in Beijing in 1993, were a window onto the outside world. But as traveling abroad has become easier, it has also lost its appeal. CNN’s Simone McCarthy explores how the park’s meaning has changed, and why it’s drawing crowds again. articles.title: Navy veteran blindsided as attacker could land parole hearing months after sentencing: ‘Where is my justice?’
articles.summary: Amy's 1992 Valentine's Day rape cold case was solved by DNA evidence, but a VINE text revealed Virginia's parole board may review her attacker.
articles.body: For 33 years, Amy has lived with the trauma of a 1992 Valentine's Day rape in Virginia, a cold case that finally cracked last year when DNA evidence linked the crime to a convicted rapist. In September 2025, Anthony Favors, 57, who initially faced six indictments, including abduction and burglary, took a plea deal for two counts of rape to secure a 24-year prison sentence. Norfolk Judge Everett A. Martin Jr. ordered 12 years for each count to run consecutively. Months later, Amy received an automated VINE text that Virginia’s parole board planned to review Favors’ case for possible release. "I finally get some sort of closure and justice. And then I get a text," Amy told Fox News Digital. "Nobody yet has told me how he's even eligible for parole." SUSAN SMITH ELIGIBLE FOR PAROLE AGAIN AFTER BEING DENIED RELEASE FOR DROWNING HER 2 SONS IN 1994 Norfolk Commonwealth’s Attorney Ramin Fatehi confirmed to Fox News Digital that Favors will likely have a "discretionary parole hearing" within the next few months. Fatehi explained that a bureaucratic overlap triggered the hearing: the parole board previously considered Favors for release on a previous rape conviction but never granted it, legally opening the door for the upcoming review. "It’s discretionary because he had been locked up for so long. He is theoretically eligible," Fatehi said. FORENSIC GENEALOGY UNMASKS COLD CASE SUSPECT AS STRANGLER, SEXUAL PREDATOR DECADES LATER: OFFICIALS Separate rape case Favors was serving a 60-year sentence for a separate March 1992 rape when a 2024 DNA hit linked him to Amy’s case. Since he committed his offenses before Jan. 1, 1995, Virginia's old sentencing laws authorized the Virginia Parole Board to consider him for release. Fatehi said that there is a "slim chance to zero" of actually releasing Favors, but the possibility of an impending hearing left Amy reeling. MAX FACTOR HEIR'S FORMER LAWYER DETAILS JUDGE'S ERROR THAT WIPED OUT 124-YEAR RAPE SENTENCE "The only word I can think of right now, honestly, is disgusting," she said. "It's wrong. How can you do that? Where is my justice?" The attack altered the course of Amy's life. Favors beat and assaulted the active-duty Navy sailor for hours at her Norfolk apartment. Despite the trauma, she reported directly to her shift on a Navy ship immediately after the attack. SERIAL KILLER SURVIVOR WHO ESCAPED 18-HOUR CAPTIVITY REVEALS INSTINCT SHE WISHES SHE NEVER IGNORED Decades later, the psychological scars have dictated her daily routine. She battles severe PTSD, chronic sleep deprivation, and hypervigilance that forces her to constantly check and recheck her door locks. "Some of the things that I did that I thought were normal, were not normal. And I still do," Amy said. "Check the locks, recheck the locks, check the locks, recheck the locks. I'm not sleeping again because... it's the unknown." CONVICTED PREDATORS FACE LIFETIME BARRIER UNDER GOP LAWMAKER’S SWEEPING VICTIM PROTECTION BILL "If you took the Amy before my rape and the Amy after my rape, I am two different people." FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X Heather Keeley, director of the nonprofit advocacy group Stand Tall, said survivors already carry the weight of their past assaults. By granting Favors a future parole hearing, she argued, the justice system actively expands that trauma by forcing victims to endlessly relive it. articles.title: Qeshm island and Hormuz hit, as mediators try to prevent US-Iran escalation
articles.summary: US strikes have continued on Iran after more ships in the Strait of Hormuz were attacked.
articles.body:
Tehran, Iran – The United States has bombed Iran after vessels were targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, as mediators continue to try to prevent large-scale fighting between the two countries.

Two projectiles hit Iran’s Qeshm on Friday night, the latest in a series of air strikes on the southern island over recent weeks targeting Iranian air defences and launchers. President Donald Trump called them “minor strikes” , amid increasing concerns of a potential escalation in the war between the countries.

Iran’s army said in the early hours of Saturday that it destroyed a US-made MQ-9 drone using an unnamed new system. The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) separately claimed on Friday that its air defences intercepted an MQ-1, reportedly the 16th aircraft of this model to be destroyed since the start of the war.

At least 11 ships were attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz over the week ending on November 6, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), which said three of them sank. The Western military intelligence agency has recorded 88 projectile strikes since hostilities resumed in early July, although it has cautioned that most attacks are going unreported .

UKMTO’s weekly report also identified 170 outbound and 155 inbound transits in the Strait of Hormuz, approximately 65 percent below pre-conflict levels. Most of the vessels that travel with their transponders switched on are using the Iranian route to the north. But many ships are still attempting the southern route near Oman with their tracking systems offline to shuttle oil out of the waterway .

Iranian armed forces also claim that, in addition to being hit with missiles and drones, tankers and commercial vessels using “unauthorised” routes also run the risk of being hit by naval mines.

The Iranian military’s naval force said on Saturday that a tanker with its transponder turned off caught fire in the eastern area of the Strait of Hormuz after hitting a mine. Washington says the mines have been cleared.

For years, the IRGC maintained that it was limiting the range of its ballistic missiles to about 2,000 kilometres (1,240 miles) to reassure European countries that they would not be targeted.

But with Trump threatening to resume extensive air strikes on Iran’s civilian infrastructure, commanders say nothing is off limits now.

“This limitation has been lifted for us,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebbi told reporters during an event on Saturday, in reference to missile range constraints.

His comments came after Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei ordered an unrestrained military response to any future threats from Israel and the US. Iran’s aerospace division of the IRGC has prepared “surprising defence achievements” that will be deployed in action if another wave of major attacks starts, he added.

“The operational unveiling of these [advanced] achievements in case of new conflict will not only frustrate and fascinate enemies, but will further solidify Iran’s military authority on the global stage, make the resistance front happy, and fully neutralise aggressors’ calculations,” Mohebbi said.

The spokesman said the IRGC plans to unveil another underground “missile city” soon, and will deploy some combat systems to public spaces so the people can personally inspect them.

Mohebbi added that if the Islamic republic decides to alter its nuclear doctrine and build a bomb, the necessary preparations will be made.

On state television’s war-focused Be Vaght-e Iran (At Iran’s Time) programme over the weekend, presenters and analysts said Iranian armed forces had their fingers on the trigger and were especially eyeing any movement from Israel.

“Our military information about the strategic chokepoints of Israel is complete. If our water, electricity and natural gas is cut off, they will also be plunged into darkness and lack of water,” one analyst said. “This is not a bluff, but a serious warning.”

Over recent weeks, diplomatic efforts by mediators to avoid attacks that could damage the entire region have picked up, although with limited gains.

Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Saturday that he held talks with 12 foreign ministers over the past 48 hours, including top diplomats from Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan.

He said he explained the “fundamental positions” of Tehran, including the seven demands to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and stressed the need to form “regional security arrangements without the interference of superregional powers”.

Security chief Mohsen Rezaei reportedly emphasised the same conditions to Russian President Vladimir Putin during a visit to Moscow on Thursday, which was also aimed at delivering a message from Khamenei.

Developments between Iran and the US resemble a “constant pendulum swing between war and negotiations” that is increasingly leaning towards conflict, according to political analyst Mostafa Najafi, who is said to be close to Iran’s security chief.

“What is clear for now is that the movement of this pendulum will continue; a conflict whose ending is much more complicated and time-consuming than imagined,” he wrote on X. The historic defeat for Trump and the Republicans in US midterm elections this week may further complicate the picture, he added.

Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft, said three factors increase the risk of war in the short term after the elections, unless negotiations lead to a breakthrough.

The political cost of high fuel prices, brought about largely due to the war on Iran, has already been paid, he said, and there won’t be another point on the political calendar soon for Trump to worry about this issue.

“On the one hand, the pressure to get a deal will dissipate,” he told Al Jazeera.

Pressure from pro-war hawks will also escalate significantly because they will be constrained in their efforts to step up the conflict after the Democrats take control of Congress in early January. The appointment of far-right, pro-Israel hawk Stephen Miller as chief of staff also hints that Trump might not be ready to wind down the war.

“Finally, there is a new psychological element to Trump’s mindset following this humiliation: Trump’s desire for vengeance. There has been a vindictive element to his calculations in the past weeks because of his anger over how Iran – in Trump’s mind – has ruined his presidency,” Parsi said.

articles.title: Pro-Russian hackers leak Italian foreign minister’s data on dark web
articles.summary: The prime minister blames pro-Russian hackers for the leak, as her top diplomat says the cyberthreat was ongoing.
articles.body:
Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said his personal data had been disseminated on the dark web, with Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blaming pro-Russian hackers for the leak.

Tajani announced in a social media post on Saturday that “for days now, cybercriminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation”.

The threats against Tajani, who is also vice prime minister of Italy, come amid a spate of hoax bomb threats across Europe that have forced flight diversions, security alerts at broadcasters, and attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems.

“They are also targeting my family; they are willing to pay for more details about me and my loved ones,” Tajani added in his X post. “My response is very simple: I will not be intimidated in any way.”

Meloni expressed solidarity with Tajani “following the revelations about the activities of pro-Russian hackers, and the publication on the dark web of personal data”.

She called attempts to sell confidential information about government officials “a matter of grave concern that must be addressed with the utmost determination”.

Tajani added in his statement that Italy’s “position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted: defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation’s democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities”.

He also suggested that the cyberthreats may also be a reaction to the Italian government’s efforts to strengthen the Foreign Ministry’s digital defences.

Tajani did not specify what kind of information had been shared, but suggested that the cyberthreat was ongoing.

He added that the ministry was taking the threats seriously and was coordinating its response with allied countries.

articles.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, says Barnier
articles.summary: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".
articles.body:
The EU's former Brexit negotiator has warned that the UK cannot "cherry pick" which elements of the single market to which it subscribes, after Andy Burnham said he wanted to explore closer economic ties with Europe.

The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago.

But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access.

He said there was not a "single market à la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt.

Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member.

But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members.

He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms".

"There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market."

Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election.

His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit.

Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime .

Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again

Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum.

Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll.

Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point.

He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship.

Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member.

The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table".

Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises."

Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. It was a lie".

The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent £350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead".

Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly £350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS".

Critics have said that the £350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's £75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK.

Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the £350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise.

​In his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only £175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money".

Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the £350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth."

articles.title: Buildings damaged in Israeli bombings risk collapse as rain inundates Gaza
articles.summary: Floods have swept through Gaza after heavy rain, endangering families and putting war-damaged buildings at risk.
articles.body:
Gaza City – Rana Adnan Hmeida, 29, stands at the entrance to her tent in al-Mina camp in northern Gaza, holding her two-month-old daughter as she tries to keep her warm after rainwater has flooded their shelter overnight. The family’s bedding, blankets and clothes are all soaked, with her children exposed to the cold and wind of Gaza’s latest storm.

Hmeida, her husband and children have been awake since midnight as heavy rain and strong winds swept through the camp. Water seeped into the tent and drenched their belongings. With all their clothes wet, Hmeida had to ask neighbours to help dry their clothes.

“Since midnight, we have been sitting awake. Water came into our tent, and the bedding, blankets and everything else got soaked. In the morning, I found my son and little daughter shivering. My two-month-old baby was freezing,” Hmeida told Al Jazeera.

“What am I supposed to do? Hold my children or try to stop the water? I was trying to keep them warm while carrying my little girl, but the water kept coming in. The wind was so strong that we felt the tent was about to be ripped out of the ground.”

Her husband, Sameh Hmeida, 30, said the family’s tent is particularly exposed due to its close proximity to the sea. It has no tarpaulins or insulating materials that might have helped in the storm.

Heavy rain has flooded camps and cities across Gaza over the past days, where many Palestinians are spending the fourth winter outside their homes since Israel began its genocidal war on the enclave in October 2023.

Water levels have risen by 30 to 40cm (12 to 16in) at several camps in Gaza due to Saturday’s rain, with Gaza’s civil defence agency receiving hundreds of calls.

Rainwater has flooded many tents in al-Mina camp, where about 1,700 Palestinian families live, turning the ground into pools of muddy water.

Raed Abu Amsha, 40, said his tent collapsed on top of his family during the storm. The clothes and blankets of all nine children in his care, four of them from his late brother, were soaked.

“I am responsible for orphans as well as my own children, and I cannot provide for their needs. This storm lasted only two hours, and look what it did to us. We need tents, tarpaulins and anything that can protect our children. How long are we going to keep living like this?” he said.

In Nuseirat, a decades-old camp in central Gaza with permanent structures, rainfall also threatens families living in buildings damaged by Israeli bombardments.

Nasser al-Hajj, 54, lives in a tower block that was hit in an Israeli strike in September 2025. Debris from upper floors fell onto his home, leaving a large hole in the ceiling where water now enters every time it rains.

Although the ceiling has been reinforced with support beams, an engineer has warned al-Hajj that the apartment is dangerous, with the risk of further rubble falling from the building if more bad weather hits Gaza.

During the latest storm, al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home and waited for the debris to stop falling from the roof. Two of his children, who have autism, sleep in the tower block’s guard room, away from the damaged area.

“I am forced to live somewhere that could collapse over our heads at any moment. But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera. “I know how dangerous this place is, but I have no other option,” he added.

According to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), about 950,000 displaced people in Gaza are living in areas exposed to flooding. Low-lying locations and sites near the coast are particularly vulnerable, with more than 400,000 people living in areas considered at high risk of flooding.

About 44,000 Palestinians are living in structurally unsafe buildings, while more than 4,000 buildings across the territory are estimated to require full or partial demolition due to damage caused by Israeli air strikes. About 294,250 families need shelter assistance ahead of winter, but the available supplies cover only 18 percent of their needs.

The Gaza Municipality is also struggling to respond to the storms. About 15 kilometres of rainwater drainage lines and 212 kilometres of sewage networks have been damaged. Eight pumping stations and three main stormwater collection basins are out of service.

The remaining system can handle no more than 20 percent of rainwater under the best of circumstances, according to municipality spokesperson Hosni Muhanna.

“[We] continue to clean drainage systems in preparation for the rainy season,” Muhanna said.

The municipality has deployed workers to clean drains and manholes, remove rubbish and clear water channels, repair damaged sections of drainage lines and operate water pumps.

But Muhanna warns that these efforts cannot restore the network’s capacity amid shortages of fuel, equipment and spare parts.

More than 2,000 buildings in Gaza City alone are at risk of collapse, he said, and the volume of rubble in Gaza City has exceeded 25 million tonnes.

Emergency committees in displacement camps are also struggling with shortages of shelter supplies. Adli Awad, an official with the emergency committee in Nuseirat refugee camp, said his team is trying to distribute tents and tarpaulins, particularly to families affected by the rain. But the number of people in need far exceeds available stocks.

“We are trying to provide as many tents and tarpaulins as possible. We are also helping families dig channels to divert rainwater away from tents and reduce flooding,” Awad said.

articles.title: New Zealand in political limbo after knife-edge election
articles.summary: New Zealand voters face weeks of political limbo after a knife-edge election that has left country’s conservative coalition government at risk of losing its majority after just a single term in office.
articles.body: New Zealand voters face weeks of political limbo after a knife-edge election left the country’s conservative coalition government at risk of losing its majority following just a single term in office. Saturday’s preliminary results show Prime Minister Christopher Luxon’s National-led coalition with a two seat majority. But the margin is so tight, a small variance in the final tally could yet leave the opposition left-wing bloc with a chance to form a government. Luxon told supporters gathered in Auckland that while it looked like his party had a pathway to form the next government, the race remained “too close to call.” He said the country would need to wait until the Electoral Commission delivered the final official results on November 27 for certainty. Coalition negotiations could then drag on for weeks before a government is formed. Preliminary numbers show the right-wing coalition grouping has 67 seats in the 131-seat parliament. Should it fall short of a majority, Luxon would likely need to turn to the progressive centrist Opportunity party, which will enter parliament for first time, for support. Prior to the election he had ruled out working with the party. The center-left Labour party received the highest share of the popular vote under the country’s mixed-member proportional voting system by a tiny margin, but a stronger performance in individual electorates has delivered National more seats in parliament. Labour Leader Chris Hipkins made light of Saturday’s inconclusive results as he addressed supporters in Wellington, saying: “Tonight, New Zealand has spoken. It may take us a little bit longer to figure out exactly what it is that you’ve said.” Hipkins, who served briefly as prime minister in 2023, did not concede, telling the crowd that “every vote matters. And every vote must be counted.” The opposition grouping of center-left Labour, the leftist Greens and indigenous party Te Pati Māori is projected to have 57 seats. But the bloc could have a path to power if it picked up some additional seats in the final count, and if it secured the support of Opportunity. Struggle for reelection The incumbent coalition – the country’s most right-wing in a generation – took power in 2023, capitalizing on an electorate looking for change in the wake of the Covid-19 pandemic. But its struggle to secure an emphatic victory this time signifies the level of public discontent over living costs, stubbornly high unemployment rates and concerns over healthcare. Luxon’s center-right National party emerges a diminished force, crashing to just 29.2% of the popular vote, down from 38.1% in 2023, according to the preliminary count. Its coalition partners, the right-wing-libertarian ACT party and the nationalist New Zealand First Party, increased their vote share to 10.9% and 9.8% respectively, putting them both in a stronger position to dictate terms in pending coalition talks. The stronger-than-expected result for New Zealand First and ACT, and National’s weakened position, raises the prospect of the coalition moving further to the right in a second term and further embracing culture-war policies. On the campaign trail the ACT vowed to end affirmative action schemes at the country’s medical schools, while New Zealand First promised sweeping immigration changes and voiced support for a review of the ban on gay conversion therapy. Luxon, would also have a complex job filling key cabinet posts in a second term, with a raft of senior lawmakers from his National party, including finance minister Nicola Willis and parliament’s speaker Gerry Brownlee, losing their seats. Voters turn to minor parties Swing voters turned away from National and Labour, which have dominated Wellington politics for nearly a century, opting to support minor parties entrenched further to the right and the left, as well as Opportunity in the center. Its political newcomer leader Qiulae Wong, 38, who applied for the party’s leadership by responding to a job advertisement a year ago, told supporters they had voted “to change New Zealand politics for good.” The party, which secured nearly 6% of the vote, becomes the first total outsider party (not involving established political figures) to enter parliament since the country moved to a mixed-member proportional voting system in the mid-1990s. Depending on the final vote tally, Opportunity, which positions itself as both business-and climate-friendly, could yet find itself in the kingmaker position – with both the right and the left groupings vying for its support.
