articles.title: With an ode to mate tea, Pope urges faithful to build bridges of fraternity and faith
articles.summary: PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, as he used his first Mass in South America to deliver an ode to the region’s beloved mate tea and raise the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country.
articles.body: PAYSANDÚ, Uruguay — Pope Leo XIV urged an estimated 40,000 people in Uruguay on Saturday to build bridges of fraternity and faith, as he used his first Mass in South America to deliver an ode to the region’s beloved mate tea and raise the profile of the Catholic Church in its most secular country. The crowd erupted in the stadium chant of “Olé, olé, olé, olé, Pope, Pope!” when Leo’s plane landed in Paysandú, in western Uruguay on the border with Argentina. They cheered again, blew horns and waved yellow handkerchiefs when he arrived in his open-sided popemobile at the Mass site in the Parque París Londres, a sprawling green space on the southern edge of Paysandú. More than 30,000 people — many from Uruguay but also from neighboring Argentina and Brazil — had registered in advance to attend the service, around 230 miles from the capital, Montevideo. The Vatican said Saturday another 10,000 had shown up beyond that, despite the morning rain and blustery, gray skies. Because of its accessible location on the Uruguay River, the city was chosen to host Leo’s first Mass at the start of his three-nation South American tour that was in doubt after he underwent lung cancer surgery on Oct. 13. Crowds of faithful in rain ponchos, many in the Vatican’s yellow, began streaming into the site when the gates opened at 5:30 a.m. as a band played popular Spanish hymns. Some in the crowd said they were deeply moved that Leo pressed on with his ambitious 12-day tour despite his recent cancer diagnosis. “He’s the representative of Christ but he’s human. And we weren’t sure if he could make it, but he pushed through for us,” said Soledad Sánchez, 73, who had driven to Paysandú from northern Uruguay, her eyes filling with tears. “He made it here to give us a message of peace because he knows our world needs it right now.” Leo, who arrived in Uruguay on Friday, is seeking to urge the people in South America’s most secular country, with a population of 3.5 million, to turn to the Catholic faith for strength in confronting today’s problems and challenges. In his homily, Leo urged the faithful to build bridges of faith, fraternity and encounter, recalling the nearby bridge over the Uruguay River that unites Uruguay and Argentina and over which many pilgrims traveled to attend the Mass. He also pointed to the ritual of drinking mate, the ubiquitous bitter herbal tea that Uruguayans and their neighbors carry everywhere, as a poignant symbol of unity and encounter that he suggested should be applied to spreading the faith today. Mate, a cherished national symbol in Paraguay, Argentina and Uruguay, is above all a sharing ritual. The leaves are steeped in a hollowed gourd and sipped through a metal straw called a bombilla, and the gourd passes from hand to hand among friends, family and sometimes strangers, refilled for hours. Everyone drinks from the same straw, and Uruguayans drink more mate per person than anyone else in the world, roughly 20 pounds of the dried leaf a year, according to industry estimates. In his comments, Leo delivered an ode to mate. “It teaches us to share and to be together, strengthening the bonds that unite us as brothers and sisters,” he said, drawing a round of applause and a smile from the pope. Symbols like mate give identity and a sense of belonging that point to the future, he said. “Faith, too, has been part of the life of the Uruguayan people since their earliest days, and it must be passed on to future generations with creative courage,” he said. Leo was to press the message of the church’s commitment to helping Uruguayans later Saturday by touring a Montevideo neighborhood beset by drug trafficking and gang violence, where the church is working with municipal authorities to build housing and provide rehab programs for addicts. His final event, too, was likely to drive home the call to reject religious indifference and embrace the faith: a prayer vigil in Montevideo’s Centenary Stadium. Located in western Uruguay and just across a bridge from the eastern Argentine city of Colón, Paysandú was easier to reach for many Argentines than any of the stops on Leo’s part of the tour in Argentina, his next stop after Uruguay. In Argentina, Leo will visit Buenos Aires, Luján and Córdoba before heading to Peru, his second homeland and the final destination of his tour. “Argentina is a much more religious country than Uruguay, and there’s this desire to be here to witness something historic,” said Luciana Lobato, 20, an Argentine tour agent who organized buses of 180 pilgrims from across the border. Some young Catholics involved in local church groups hoped the sight of a pope drawing crowds would challenge Uruguay’s image as a country indifferent to religion. “The reality I see in my town is that there are tons of young people who are really interested in religion, who are trying to find meaning and community in difficult moments,” said Teresa Sabellini, 18, from Paysandú. “And now look around here. This place is full of people,” she added. Still, Paysandú itself greeted the pope quietly, as though it were an ordinary weekend, with scant decorations and only a few homes seen flying Vatican flags. Saturday’s Mass was dedicated to Blessed Jacinto Vera, a 19th-century priest who became Uruguay’s first bishop. Leo praised him on Friday as a pastor who traveled the country’s roads to help the poor, saying that people who met him “found something of Christ’s goodness” even before he preached. Some younger attendees on Saturday said Leo’s humane tone and emphasis on care for the vulnerable resonated beyond the faithful in their secular country as people grapple with a turbulent world. “I wouldn’t call myself religious, but I like this pope. He has a really good message for humanity,” said Santiago Biglieri, 18, a Colombian who lives in Uruguay. “Even for the nonbelievers, there’s something to take from his ideas.”

articles.title: Nazi spies landed on US soil days before a German U-boat sank a Canadian ship off Maine in 1944; 82 years later, divers uncover the long-lost wreck 400 feet below the Atlantic
articles.summary: A German submarine secretly landed two Nazi spies on American soil in November 1944 before torpedoing a Canadian merchant ship off the coast of Maine just
articles.body: A German submarine secretly landed two Nazi spies on American soil in November 1944 before torpedoing a Canadian merchant ship off the coast of Maine just four days later, killing 43 people aboard. More than eight decades after the World War II tragedy, divers have finally located the long-lost vessel nearly 400 feet beneath the Atlantic Ocean. The discovery of the SS Cornwallis, reported by Smithsonian Magazine, has brought renewed attention to one of the lesser-known episodes of Nazi espionage along America's eastern coastline.The wreck was discovered on July 11, 2026, by the Nomad Exploration Team, a civilian technical diving group based in Portsmouth, New Hampshire. The team had spent seven years searching for the missing ship before locating it near Mount Desert Rock in the Gulf of Maine. Using side-scan sonar, historical shipping records and the vessel's original blueprints, the divers identified the wreck in approximately 400 feet of water.The discovery was formally announced in October, more than 81 years after the ship disappeared beneath the sea. The team said locating the vessel was not just an achievement in underwater exploration but also an opportunity to bring attention to the 43 people who lost their lives.The ship that was torpedoed twice during World War IIThe SS Cornwallis was a 5,458-ton steam merchant vessel built in Vancouver, British Columbia, in 1921. Originally named Canadian Transporter, it was later renamed Cornwallis after becoming part of Canadian National Steamships. Its wartime history was already unusual. On September 11, 1942, the vessel was attacked by a German submarine while anchored in Barbados. The torpedoes severely damaged the ship, causing it to partially sink in shallow water. However, it was subsequently refloated, repaired and returned to service.Two years later, the Cornwallis was once again sailing through waters where German submarines posed a threat. In November 1944, it departed Barbados carrying sugar and molasses bound for Saint John, New Brunswick. There were 48 people aboard, including seven armed guards.On December 3, 1944, as the vessel travelled along the Maine coastline, German submarine U-1230 spotted it and launched a torpedo. The explosion struck near the forward cargo hold, causing the ship to sink by the bow in less than 10 minutes. Only five of the 48 people aboard survived. Six initially managed to reach life rafts, but one subsequently died from hypothermia. The remaining survivors were eventually spotted and rescued by fishing boats before being transferred to a US Navy rescue vessel, which took them to Rockland, Maine.Nazi spies who secretly landed in MaineWhat makes the Cornwallis sinking particularly unusual is the identity of the submarine responsible. The U-1230, commanded by German naval officer Hans Hilbig, had arrived off the Maine coast with a secret intelligence mission just days before attacking the merchant vessel. On the night of November 29, 1944, the submarine entered Frenchman Bay and brought two German agents ashore near Crabtree Neck in Hancock, Maine. The operation was part of a Nazi espionage mission intended to gather intelligence about American industrial and technological capabilities.The two agents were Erich Gimpel, a 35-year-old German national, and William Curtis Colepaugh, a 26-year-old American-born Nazi sympathiser who had travelled to Germany and received espionage training. They had boarded the U-1230 in Germany and crossed the Atlantic before being dropped off on the Maine coastline. According to the US Navy's Eastern Sea Frontier War Diary, the submarine surfaced partially at around 10:30 pm and approached to within approximately 300 yards of the shore. Two German sailors then used a rubber boat to transport the agents to land before returning to the submarine.The operation was carried out without the coastal authorities detecting the landing. The spies subsequently made their way towards Bangor, travelled by train to Portland and eventually reached New York City. The agents reportedly carried approximately $60,000 in cash, diamonds, forged identification documents and secret inks. Their assignment was to collect information about American industrial facilities and technological developments during the war. Their mission, however, did not go according to plan.Colepaugh eventually had second thoughts about his involvement and turned himself in to the FBI on December 26, 1944. His cooperation helped investigators locate Gimpel, who was arrested in New York on December 30. Both men were convicted of espionage and initially sentenced to death by a military court. Their sentences were later commuted by US President Harry Truman.How the sinking exposed the secret submarine missionThe connection between the spy landing and the Cornwallis attack became an important part of the subsequent investigation. According to the US Navy's wartime records, American authorities had anticipated that a German submarine might enter the Gulf of Maine. Precautionary air patrols were conducted in the region during November 1944, but no enemy submarine was detected.It was only after the Cornwallis was torpedoed on December 3 that officials could suspect that the submarine responsible might also have been involved in landing German agents near Mount Desert. The incident also demonstrated how close the German submarine campaign had come to the US mainland, even as the country was heavily involved in fighting the war overseas.Seven-year search leads divers to the missing shipThe search for the Cornwallis began in 2019, when the Nomad Exploration Team decided to locate what was considered one of the largest missing shipwrecks in New England waters. The team studied historical records, examined archived blueprints and consulted maritime historians and local fishermen to narrow down the possible location. Researchers identified three potential search areas based on where survivors were rescued, where debris had been reported and where a mariner claimed to have recovered the ship's compass housing.The divers eventually scanned more than 50 square miles of the ocean floor using side-scan sonar. During their July 2026 expedition, the team spotted a possible wreck on July 11, although it initially passed the location without recognising the vessel. A subsequent sonar scan revealed the ship's outline. The divers then undertook deep-water expeditions to establish its identity, using the original blueprints to confirm that it was the Cornwallis.The confirmation was far from easy. The wreck lies nearly 400 feet underwater, where divers had to contend with extremely cold temperatures, powerful currents and difficult visibility. Team members described the dives as some of the most challenging they had undertaken in their years of technical diving.For the discovery team, the excitement of locating a missing World War II vessel was accompanied by the realisation that they were exploring the final resting place of 43 people. Danny Allan, a founding member of the Nomad Exploration Team, told the Portland Press Herald that the discovery could bring renewed attention and a sense of closure to the families connected to the tragedy.The team has said it hopes to return to the site and use a remotely operated underwater vehicle to document the wreck and monitor its deterioration. The divers have also indicated that they do not intend to claim ownership of the vessel, describing the discovery itself and the opportunity to put the missing ship back on the map as their greatest reward.You use AI every day. articles.title: Tiger Woods' former mistress Rachel Uchitel spends $100,000 on cosmetic surgery makeover after years of facial fillers and aesthetic treatments left her unhappy with her appearance
articles.summary: Rachel Uchitel, who became an international tabloid sensation after being linked to golf legend Tiger Woods in 2009, has reportedly spent $100,000 on an
articles.body: Rachel Uchitel, who became an international tabloid sensation after being linked to golf legend Tiger Woods in 2009, has reportedly spent $100,000 on an extensive cosmetic surgery makeover. The 51-year-old podcast host underwent several procedures in August after admitting that years of facial fillers and aesthetic treatments had left her unhappy with her appearance. She said she wanted to move away from an overfilled look and achieve a fresher, more natural appearance.Uchitel opened up about her transformation in an interview with the Daily Mail. Reflecting on her past cosmetic treatments, she admitted that she had gone too far with fillers, saying she had 'f--ed up her face'. Before undergoing surgery, she spent two weeks having the existing fillers dissolved to prepare for the procedures.Uchitel told the publication that the procedure took 11 and a half hours, although she was under anaesthesia for nine hours. However, she also described the operation as lasting nine and a half hours in an Instagram post.The makeover was performed by board-certified plastic surgeon Dr Ira Savetsky. The procedures included a deep-plane facelift, a tightening brow lift, under-eye fat transfer, chin fat transfer and a columella nose revision.Rather than simply adding more volume to her face, the surgical plan focused on addressing the effects of previous cosmetic treatments and restoring her facial proportions. Dr Savetsky explained that Uchitel wanted to move away from the overfilled appearance that had developed after years of aesthetic procedures.'Rachel came to me with a very clear goal: she wanted to move away from the overfilled appearance she had developed over years of aesthetic treatments and return to a more natural, balanced version of herself,' he told the publication.Doctor reveals why Rachel Uchitel's surgery was complicatedDr Savetsky also revealed that the operation was more complicated than a routine facelift because of changes to Uchitel's facial tissues. Years of fillers and energy-based skin-tightening treatments had left dense scar tissue and adhesions in several areas. Despite the two weeks of filler-dissolving treatments before surgery, the doctor said he encountered residual filler during the operation.Instead of relying on additional injectable fillers, Savetsky used Uchitel's own fat to restore volume in selected areas. He explained that microfat was used to rebuild subtle facial volume, while nanofat helped improve skin quality and the appearance of delicate tissues.Photographs taken after her fillers were dissolved but before surgery were compared with images captured approximately eight weeks after the makeover. Uchitel said she was pleased with the results and had already received positive reactions from people she met in Palm Beach, Florida, where she lives with her husband, Dan Donovan.'Everyone is like, "Wow, you look amazing." And the word isn't, "Oh, you had something done." The word is, "You look really refreshed!"' she said.Rachel Uchitel opens up about ageing and cosmetic treatmentsUchitel also spoke about the stigma surrounding cosmetic treatments and ageing, arguing that women should not feel embarrassed about wanting to maintain their appearance.'There's so much shame around ageing and beauty, and what is beautiful and what is natural, right?' she said, adding that people should feel comfortable maintaining their appearance according to their own preferences.'I'm 51. I just got married. I care about what I look like.'Interestingly, her husband was also impressed by the results. Uchitel revealed that Donovan subsequently visited Savetsky for a brow lift of his own. The surgeon believes her decision to move away from excessive fillers reflects a wider shift in cosmetic surgery preferences, with more patients seeking subtle enhancements instead of exaggerated facial volume.'Rachel didn't want a new face. She wanted her own face back,' he explained.Rachel Uchitel's relationship with Tiger Woods: What happened in 2009?Uchitel first came into the international spotlight in November 2009, when reports linked her to married professional golfer Tiger Woods. At the time, she denied having an affair with him and called the allegations untrue. However, the controversy soon became a major part of the scandal surrounding Woods' personal life and marriage to Swedish model Elin Nordegren.Years later, Uchitel spoke about her relationship with Woods in the 2021 HBO documentary Tiger, offering her account of how they met and what happened between them. She also discussed the intense media scrutiny she faced after the story became public.Woods subsequently issued a public apology for his infidelity in February 2010. His marriage to Nordegren ended in divorce in August that year. The golfer's personal life remained under intense media attention following the revelations, while Uchitel's name continued to be associated with the scandal.You use AI every day. articles.title: Heavy rain floods thousands of tents in Gaza, aid shortages hamper response
articles.summary: Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians crammed into encampments across the Gaza Strip, washing away shelters and soaking blankets and mattresses, local authorities said on Saturday.
articles.body: Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents housing displaced Palestinians crammed into encampments across the Gaza Strip, washing away shelters and soaking blankets and mattresses, local authorities said on Saturday. The Hamas-run Gaza government ⁠media office said at least 70,000 tents had been flooded in the past 12 hours, affecting tens of thousands of displaced people and causing injuries, although no fatalities had been reported. The territory’s civil defence service said it had received 1,500 distress calls from displaced residents. Three abandoned houses collapsed without causing injuries, it added. At a tent encampment in Gaza City, some people tried to repair their tents, ⁠while others used sand to reinforce them and prevent water from ​entering. ⁠Some were busy getting their children out of flooded tents. Olfat Magdoub, a Gaza resident, tried in vain to sweep water away from her tent. “This is the first day of rain, and of course ⁠we are already flooded. What will happen if it rains again the next day? This is only the first ​day and ⁠we’re already overwhelmed,” said the woman. “Two weeks ago ‌when it rained, I swear to God, I spent four days sleeping on blankets spread on the floor because the rainwater had flooded the bedding. Same now, the mattresses are wet so we sleep on the ground.” Municipal and ‌civil defence officials said they were unable to cope with the storm ‌because of fuel shortages and damage to equipment. They said Israel had destroyed hundreds of vehicles, including bulldozers and others used to pump water, during its war against Hamas, which had displaced most of the territory’s more than 2 million residents and left much of Gaza in ruins. Most of the ⁠population now lives in tent camps. Hamas blamed Israel for not allowing shelters and construction materials into Gaza. COGAT, the Israeli military agency that coordinates aid, did not immediately comment on the accusations by Hamas. It said in a statement on Friday that it had stepped up efforts to improve sanitary conditions across Gaza before the heavy rain, which had been expected, in coordination with international organisations. The agency said four additional vacuum trucks entered Gaza this week through the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), joining eight others brought in over the past month to support ‌sewage pumping, weekly waste removal and repairs to water and sewage infrastructure. A U.S.-brokered ceasefire last year ​called for the eventual reconstruction of Gaza, but little progress has been made. Negotiators have failed to agree ‌on terms for Hamas to disarm or for Israel ⁠to withdraw its troops, which control about two-thirds of the territory and from which residents have ⁠been ordered to leave. “We have no resources, no tarpaulins, no tents and no one is checking on us,” said displaced Gaza resident Rafiq Ghattas, standing barefoot ‌in the middle of a ​large pool of rainwater. Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 ‌people have been killed in Gaza since Israel began its ​assault on the territory after Hamas-led fighters killed about 1,200 people in southern Israel on attacks on October 7, 2023.

articles.title: Baxters fish soup cans recalled over fears they could 'swell and rupture'
articles.summary: A manufacturing fault could cause a batch of the Cullen Skink soup to spoil, and cans could swell and burst.
articles.body:
Customers who bought cans of a fish soup manufactured by Baxters have been urged to dispose of them in outside bins over fears the tins could burst.

The firm has recalled its Chef Selections Cullen Skink soup, a smoked haddock chowder, due to a manufacturing fault which may cause it to spoil and cans to "swell and potentially rupture", according to the Food Standards Agency (FSA).

If spoilt, the soup may have an "unpleasant odour and flavour", the FSA said.

The company, based in the north east of Scotland, said the issue may affect the 400g cans with batch code L07XC and an April 2029 best before date.

Shoppers who bought the soup in England, Wales and Scotland have been told not to eat it, and to instead dispose of it without opening it.

"Carefully place the full can in a bag and dispose of it in an external bin," the FSA told customers.

People seeking a replacement are told to contact Baxters customer care team at ccuk@baxters.com.

Founded in Fochabers in Moray in 1868, Baxters remains one of Scotland's best-known food manufacturers.

It remains a privately-owned family business and is now run by fourth-generation family member Audrey Baxter.

articles.title: At least five dead in shooting in the main market square of Krakow, Poland, police say
articles.summary: At least five people have been killed and about a dozen more injured in a shooting incident in the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on Saturday afternoon, according to Polish police.
articles.body: At least five people have been killed and about a dozen more injured in a shooting incident in the main market square of Krakow, Poland, on Saturday afternoon, according to Polish police. The shooting occurred at around 3 p.m. local time (9 a.m. ET), when a man drove onto the square and opened fire from within his vehicle at what appeared to be random people, Krakow police said in a post on X. The suspected perpetrator was shot by police and has been transported to the hospital, police said. Emergency services are still working at the scene, police said in another update. Police officers are among those injured. Heavily armed police wearing helmets and tactical gear are present at the square, video footage from Reuters showed. Pedestrians can be seen walking down the street as sirens ring out in the background. Krakow’s main market square, lined with cafes and bars, is typically a busy area that is popular with tourists. Polish Prime ​Minister ‌Donald Tusk ​said in a social media post that police are investigating ​the “tragic shooting” ⁠and that he is ⁠being ‌updated by ‌the interior ‌ministry. Poland, like most European Union countries, has strict rules about acquiring guns and very few people are allowed to own guns or carry them in public. This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

articles.title: ‘There’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet’: Woman’s niece discovers 1930 painting hidden for four decades in New York apartment; rare artwork, once bought for $3,800, could now fetch $3 million at auction
articles.summary: A casual remark about an old painting tucked away in a closet has led to an extraordinary art-world discovery: a long-unseen work by American modernist
articles.body: A casual remark about an old painting tucked away in a closet has led to an extraordinary art-world discovery: a long-unseen work by American modernist Georgia O’Keeffe, valued at around $3 million, is heading to auction after spending nearly four decades out of public view in a New York apartment. The painting, 'Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I', was found by the niece of its owner, who had reportedly kept it packed in its original box after becoming uneasy when a guest appeared to pay it too much attention during a bridge game in the 1980s.The owner’s revelation was disarmingly matter-of-fact. “Oh, by the way, there’s a Georgia O’Keeffe in the closet,” she reportedly told her niece. The family had not known about the artwork’s existence until then. After the owner died, her niece contacted Christie’s, setting in motion the process that brought the painting back into the art market and public view.According to People, the 10-by-24-inch oil painting was created in 1930 and depicts Lobo Peak in New Mexico. Christie’s estimates its value at around $3 million. It will be offered at the auction house’s 20th Century Evening Sale in New York on November 17, 2026, after being displayed in a public exhibition from November 7 to 17 at Christie’s Rockefeller Center premises.The story behind the painting stretches back to 1963, when the owner’s mother purchased it for $3,800 from The Downtown Gallery in Manhattan, which represented O’Keeffe. The artwork was given to her daughter as a graduation present after she earned a master’s degree. For a time, it was displayed in her East Village apartment, but that changed in the mid-1980s.During a bridge game, the owner noticed that a guest appeared to be looking at the painting rather closely. The family told the auction house that she became uncomfortable and decided to put it away. She returned it to its original box and placed it in the back of a closet, where it remained for decades.The woman was described by relatives as sophisticated and highly intelligent. She had studied at several distinguished institutions and travelled widely while working in the Foreign Service. Her family has requested that her identity remain private. The painting's rediscovery came towards the end of her life, and her niece eventually reached out to Christie’s to establish what the family had found.What makes the discovery particularly significant is that the painting was not simply an artwork missing from a family's collection. According to Christie’s, its existence had previously been documented through a photograph taken in 1931. The work appeared in the artist’s catalogue raisonné, the comprehensive scholarly record of her paintings, but had remained out of public view for decades.The auction house believes 'Near Abiquiu, New Mexico I' is probably the first of three paintings in which O’Keeffe depicted Lobo Peak. The mountain is located near Abiquiu, the northern New Mexico community that became closely associated with the artist and her work. O’Keeffe first visited New Mexico in 1929, and the region's mountains, desert landscapes and distinctive light would become recurring subjects in her paintings.The other two versions offer an indication of the significance of the rediscovered work. A second painting from 1930 is in the collection of New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art. The third, created in 1931, once belonged to collectors Peggy and David Rockefeller. Christie’s sold that version in 2018 for $8.41 million, well above its pre-sale estimate of $3 million to $5 million.Christie’s has described the newly rediscovered painting as an important early landscape that anticipates O’Keeffe’s later explorations of abstraction and the New Mexico environment. Its flowing contours and earthy colours reflect the artist’s interest in transforming familiar natural forms into compositions that could appear almost abstract.O’Keeffe, born in Wisconsin in 1887, became one of the most influential figures in American modernism. She was known for her close-up flower paintings, architectural subjects and landscapes, particularly those inspired by New Mexico. She eventually made the state her home and continued to paint its terrain throughout her career. She died in Santa Fe in 1986, aged 98.The rediscovery also comes against the backdrop of a strong market for O’Keeffe's work. Her painting 'Jimson Weed/White Flower No. 1' sold for $44.4 million at Sotheby’s in 2014, setting an auction record for the artist. The 2018 Rockefeller sale, which included the other version of 'Near Abiquiu, New Mexico', further demonstrated the demand for important works from her New Mexico period.Tylee Abbott, Christie’s senior specialist and head of American Art, described the discovery as a rare opportunity in a market where major works by established artists are generally well documented. He said the painting represented O’Keeffe’s engagement with the landscape and was remarkably well preserved.For the public, the rediscovery offers a chance to see a work that had effectively vanished from view for generations. Christie’s exhibition at 20 Rockefeller Plaza will run from November 7 to November 17, ahead of the auction. The sale proceeds are expected to be shared among family interests, with a portion also going towards an educational institution, according to reports.A painting bought for $3,800 as a graduation gift, hidden after an unsettling moment at a bridge table and remembered through a photograph for decades, is now returning to the spotlight. Nearly a century after O’Keeffe painted the New Mexico landscape, the work is set to be seen again, this time, by collectors and art lovers who may help determine its multimillion-dollar value.You use AI every day. articles.title: Iran’s IRGC says building underground sites for weapons production, storage
articles.summary: IRGC says underground military complexes allow missile production to continue even under heavy bombardment.
articles.body:
Iran is building underground military complexes able to sustain weapons production and storage even under heavy bombardment, according to the country’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) .

IRGC spokesperson Hossein Mohebbi made a series of announcements on Saturday about the military’s capabilities during a news conference in Tehran, Iranian media reported.

Among the achievements listed were an “underground missile city” set to be unveiled, the semi-official Tasnim news agency reported.

Mohebbi said the IRGC had rapidly transferred its missile and drone production lines from the surface to underground facilities. This allows Iran to continue producing missiles while its adversaries assumed its stockpiles were dwindling, he explained.

The spokesperson also outlined advances in stealth technology. He maintained that such improvements had allowed Iran’s missiles and drones to pierce air defence systems and accurately strike targets during previous rounds of fighting with the United States and Israel.

“Today, every weapon used by the IRGC Aerospace Force is manufactured using homegrown knowledge and expertise. Moreover, our products are not even derived from reverse-engineering captured enemy war material,” Iran’s IRNA news agency quoted Mohebbi as saying.

A recent report by US newspaper, The Wall Street Journal, shows that Iran caused billions of dollars in damage to US bases throughout the Middle East during previous rounds of fighting.

Meanwhile, a separate report by the Reuters news agency found that Iran had successfully targeted Gulf infrastructure on at least 135 occasions during the same period, causing billions of dollars in damage and lost revenues.

Mohebbi also warned on Saturday that restrictions on the range of Iranian missiles had been lifted. The warning follows a statement from Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who said that there would be “ no geographical limits ” to Iran’s response if it were attacked again by the US and Israel.

The US-Israeli war on Iran was launched on February 28, prompting Tehran to close the Strait of Hormuz and triggering a global energy crisis. Mediation efforts have stepped up recently, as regional countries hope to bring the war to an end.

On Friday, President Donald Trump said the US military launched limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm Island, while also claiming Washington had made “a lot of progress” in talks with Iran.

Tehran has repeatedly warned that it will target Gulf energy infrastructure if the fighting resumes. Such attacks would likely push energy prices even higher.

Meanwhile, Washington has also imposed additional sanctions on Iran as it seeks to force Tehran to concede to its demands. The restrictions have further strained the country’s economy, forcing Iran to adopt new trade routes.

On Saturday, US Central Command (CENTCOM) announced it was establishing a new task force that will support ongoing US efforts to prevent Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons and other materials.

The US has also imposed a naval blockade on Iran to prevent it from exporting oil.

articles.title: 17-yr-old shot dead in city after group clash
articles.summary: 17-year-old shot dead in Bhubaneswar’s Bomikhal after rival group clash; police arrest 7, including a minor, and seize firearm as probe continues.
articles.body: Bhubaneswar: A 17-year-old boy was allegedly shot dead at point-blank range in a retaliatory attack at Bomikhal here early on Saturday, prompting swift police action that led to the arrest of seven persons, including a minor, within hours of the incident.According to police, the deceased, identified as a child in conflict with law (CCL) of Haldiapadia, sustained a gunshot injury on his head and collapsed on the spot. Police rushed him to a nearby facility, but doctors declared him brought dead. The accused were identified as Satyajit Behera (18), Kunu Ratan (18), Manoj Behera (18), Dibya Kumbhar (19), Biswajit Hati (19), Lipun Jena (32) and one minor.According to investigators, the killing was the culmination of a clash between two groups with a history of past enmity. Preliminary findings suggested that the deceased and some of his associates allegedly disrupted a feast being hosted by the rival group. During the confrontation, bombs were reportedly hurled at the gathering, escalating tensions.DCP Sarvana Vivek said the attack was carried out in retaliation immediately after the alleged bombing. “The deceased CCL and his friends hurled bombs at the party the other group was having. At the spur of the moment, from a very close range one from the group shot Sonu,” he said.Police said a single bullet struck the deceased in the head, proving fatal. Officers have seized the firearm allegedly used in the crime. Investigators are examining whether additional shots were fired and are working to reconstruct the sequence of events leading to the murder.Police commissioner S Dev Datta Singh said the force moved quickly, arresting four suspects even before an FIR was formally lodged. Three more persons were later taken into custody after registration of the case.“There was previous enmity between the two groups, although verification revealed that none except one had criminal antecedents. Even the deceased did not have a criminal past. Investigation is continuing and anyone else found involved will be arrested,” Singh said.The commissioner attributed such violent flare-ups to issues of ego and temperament, noting that the police are attempting to strengthen engagement with slum communities and improve intelligence gathering to prevent crimes through timely intervention.Police believe the two rival groups challenged each other during the confrontation, ultimately leading to the fatal shooting. articles.title: US offers millions for information on Iran’s nuclear program despite Trump’s claims of obliteration
articles.summary: The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program, despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated claims to have obliterated Tehran’s capabilities.
articles.body: The United States is offering a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran’s nuclear program, despite US President Donald Trump’s repeated claims to have obliterated Tehran’s capabilities. Rewards for Justice (RFJ), a State Department program, is seeking tips on Iran’s nuclear facilities, equipment and associated personnel, the program said in a Friday social media post, which stated that relocation may be offered to informants. During the 12-day conflict last year, Trump was quick to declare that Iran’s key nuclear enrichment facilities had been “completely and totally obliterated.” He kept up this assessment on several occasions after and attacked media organizations — including CNN — for challenging the claim. This year’s conflict saw the US and Israel again attack Iranian nuclear sites, and Trump has made fresh claims to have tackled Iran’s threat, telling reporters on Friday that “if we didn’t hit Iran, you wouldn’t have Israel today.” But the State Department’s move — and independent assessments — suggest that concerns remain over Iran’s program, which Tehran has always insisted is peaceful. Last year, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) reported that Iran was enriching uranium to 60% purity which is “a short technical step from the 90% required for a nuclear weapon,” according to an RFJ statement. “Iran is the only non-nuclear-weapon state to produce uranium at such a high enrichment level. Experts estimate this quantity, if enriched further, could be enough for several nuclear weapons,” it said. It also referred to a “loss of continuity of knowledge regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges” due to the regime’s lack of compliance with the IAEA. Preventing Iran from developing a nuclear weapon has been stated as a key objective for Washington’s war with Iran. This week, President Donald Trump repeated claims that the US “might have to go after” Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain, the suspected underground nuclear site where Israel believes Tehran has stored part of its enriched uranium stockpile and advanced enrichment centrifuges. In response, Iran warned that that any US attack on Iranian nuclear facilities would be treated as an expansion of the war in the region. Tehran maintains that it has the right to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes, including enrichment. RFJ has also offered rewards for information on senior Iranian regime figures since the war began in February. Mediators are continuing to try to broker an agreement between Iran and the US but both sides appear unwilling to shift on key red lines, with Tehran seeing the ability to enrich uranium a matter of national sovereignty. Trump ordered new strikes on Iran overnight, describing them as “minor”. In a separate development, CENTCOM has launched a task force with the intention of preventing Iran from accessing land routes that might facilitate the transportation of advanced weapons and other materials. A naval blockade is already in place as part of US efforts to choke off Iran’s vital oil industry.

articles.title: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
articles.summary: Heavy rain has flooded temporary shelters used by Palestinians displaced during Israel's war with Hamas.
articles.body:
Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help.

Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter.

Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil.

Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation.

Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season.

Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate.

"We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help."

The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical.

Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts.

"We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said.

"But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help."

Veitch said aid workers were being "stopped on the street" by Gazans "begging us for help".

He continued: "They're absolutely desperate. We saw last year what winter does, and we had deaths from hypothermia last year.

"We can expect the same again unless we have very, very urgent action now."

A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day.

Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed.

Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled.

The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war.

The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage.

Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry.
